That, further to the Order adopted on Monday, October 29,
1990,
A Special Committee of the House of Commons on Canada-United States air transport services be appointed;
That the Committee have all the powers of a Standing Committee;
That the Committee have the power to travel and adjourn from place to place within Canada and to travel to Washington and that the necessary staff do accompany the Committee; and
That the Committee submit its report no later than January 15,
1991,	provided that, if the House is not sitting, the report will be deemed submitted on the day such report is deposited with the Clerk of the House of Commons.

That this House urge that in the upcoming GATT negotiations and in over-all economic policies, the government recognize the essential role played by farmers in maintaining the Canadian way of life and urge the government to uphold the principles of supply management, to maintain the "safety nets" to provide a stable and fair return for all sectors involved in food production, to adopt policies encouraging sustainable development in farming practices, and to recognize the vital role played by agricultural communities to the over-all economy and the well-being of all Canadians.

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. There have been some discussions in this party about the length of speeches today. As you know, our speeches are normally 20 minutes, with a 10 minute question and comment period. November 2, 1990
Supply

Madam Speaker, there is a serious crisis in our agricultural industry and rural Canada is suffering. At no time in recent history since the Depression have farmers been in such dire straits and Canadians want to know what the government is doing about it.
The production of food has always been a challenge, a challenge which farmers have continually met with adaptability and, I must say, much courage. Farm families have always had to deal with uncertainty, uncertainty caused by weather and by depressed markets.
Wheat farmers have just finished a harvest of bumper crops but with increasingly low prices we continually have reports of producers who will be forced off the land before this fall.
The government continues to talk about a new vision in agriculture in Canada. It is this new vision that has farmers concerned. What does the government mean by this new vision? One of the main corner-stones of this vision, as outlined in the government's Growing Together proposal, is centred around greater self-reliance in the agri-food industry.
Low prices are a result of a number of factors: continued U.S. and European export subsidies, the embargo against Iraq, the likelihood of a record world crop this year, and a stronger Canadian dollar. The farmer has no control over any of these.
In order to prevent financial disaster in rural Ontario and Canada, the federal government must step in now. An announcement of a special grains program to compensate for the effects of the embargo and/or an interim payment of at least $15 to $20 per tonne under the Agricultural Stabilization Act is essential. This government cannot continue to play this wait-and-see game. For too long now, farmers have been put off to face their bankers alone and to try to provide for their families with incomes far below the cost required to put food on the tables of our nation.
The government continually tries to assure farmers that greater self-reliance does not mean eliminating government support. Yet, what are farmers to expect when, in the last budget, the federal government cut down its share of the crop insurance cost-sharing program, terminated the at and east, terminated the branch
line rehabilitation program, removed the interest-free provision on the prairie grains advanced payments, and eliminated the special dairy export? The budget for the Canadian Dairy Commission's skim milk powder marketing costs and CDC operating costs were abolished. The commodity-based program which provided subsidized loans to low-equity Farm Credit Corporation clients in financial difficulty was abolished. The rebate of the excise tax for on-farm fuel was abolished. This is the type of support that this government promises, the policy of abandonment. Or is this, Madam Speaker, the policy of self-reliance?
To make matters worse, farmers like other Canadians are reeling from the government's policies of high interest rates. Increased fuel prices add an additional financial burden to an industry floundering to keep its head above water.
The government fails to realize or even admit the serious financial stress being experienced by our grain, oilseeds, horticultural, and livestock producers. The situation is acute and, although a direct consequence of low prices and actions by foreign governments, the federal government must also bear its share of responsibility for the failure to present proper safety net support programs to correct for the resulting income deprivation experienced by our Canadian farmers.
Producers welcome the opportunity to provide remedies to the safety net committee's reports. However, the report and all the work and effort of the past months will only work and only be worth-while if these proposals are implemented beginning in the 1991-92 crop year and if the costs to producers are held to a maximum of one-third of the total premium cost, in order to assure a high participation rate by our farmers.
It is imperative the gross revenue insurance plan, GRIP, and the Net Income Stabilization Account, NISA, programs proposed by the grain and oilseeds safety net committee, give the same support benefits to on-farm-fed and grain crop silage as with commercially marketed grain. It is also critical that safety net support, whether in the form of GRIP or NISA, or both, be offered to horticultural producers, many of whom are ineligible for any type of stabilization or crop insurance programs at present.

Equally important is that the financial shortfalls experienced in 1989-90 and 1990-91 be addressed if many farmers are going to be around in order to participate in these safety net programs.
I must commend the Minister of Agriculture for backing down from his previous short-sighted decision to eliminate the interest-free cash advances. His recent decision to reinstate interest-free cash advances for the first $50,000 advance for grain, oilseed and horticultural growers for 1990-91 is long overdue. This decision will partially alleviate the cash flow needs this fall, but to impose the same ceiling on the amount of interest-free assistance for multi-farmer units, such as partnerships or family corporations, as they do for individual operations will unfairly penalize those farmers who have chosen to farm collectively.
I hope the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Agriculture are listening as this change of heart will only delay and not prevent the financial stresses associated with the low prices of 1990-91. These interest-free cash advances will not negate the need for another ad hoc program in 1990-91.
It is good to see that this government has admitted it was wrong. While they are still at it, perhaps the Minister of Finance will admit that he is wrong about the GST and withdraw it. Speaking of the GST, it is just one more cross that Canadian farmers have to bear.
Farmers can carry a heavier load. They are already bearing more than their share. This is what I mean by the government recognizing the essential role played by our farmers and the vital role played by agricultural communities to the over-all economy and the well-being of all Canadians. This government will try to say it has supported our agricultural industry, but actions speak louder than words. The previous examples clearly do not substantiate these claims.
What about their new vision for agriculture respecting our supply managed sector? Again, they claim to fully support supply management. Their Growing Together paper stated, and I quote: "The national supply-management system is a uniquely Canadian system designed to strengthen farmer bargaining power and stabilize prices. It has been highly successful at reducing producer risk, increasing stability and providing market security". I
Supply
agree. Is that not what we are trying to accomplish in all other sectors?
In the GATT negotiations it appears that all the programs are on the table. We have a trade minister who tells the Minister of Agriculture that he should be ashamed of the amount of money we spend to assist farmers. How can we expect negotiators to stand up for Canadian farmers when the minister they report to thinks farmers are getting too much money? With a trade minister like that on our side at the bargaining table, who needs opponents? It is no wonder we got such a bad deal with the free trade agreement.
To add insult to injury, we have a Minister of Agriculture who gave misleading agricultural subsidy figures to GATT. When supply management was first implemented under GATT, it was understood that subsidies were something that came out of the tax base, but now the U.S. in particular is trying to argue that if consumers pay more than the world price, that is a subsidy. That is economic nonsense and this government seems to be falling for it.
The minister knows that it is inaccurate and unfair to see the price differential between Canadian and world milk prices as a subsidy for dairy farmers. Such a calculation is irrelevant and unfair because the world prices reflect dumping by countries of their subsidized surplus production. The fact is that world prices are far below the actual production costs for most dairy producing countries.
Our supply management system was implemented within the international law under Article XI of GATE We have every right to keep our system as is, but instead of defending our rights to maintain our supply management, they have undermined our own negotiating position. Our system produces a high quality production for our market at a fair and reasonable price to the consumer and provides a fair return to the producer as well. Perhaps equally important is Canada is now nearly self-sufficient in dairy products.
There is so much more I could say about the desperate needs of our agricultural sector, but my time is short. The most important industry in Canada is food production. Farmers are only asking for what other Canadians want; the right to earn a good living and support their families.

Supply
By hard work and struggling, we have built an agricultural industry that is envied the world over. We must not allow it to be destroyed by short sighted policies and short sighted politicians.

Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague for beginning this debate today on a sector of our economy that is vital.
The question that I would like to address to my colleague has to do with the youth who seem to be leaving farms right across the country. In our area in southern Ontario, the attractiveness of large industry is pulling experienced youth away from the farm.
Mothers and fathers who are just about at that age when they would like to take life a little easier are finding that they cannot take it easier because the resources are not there to help continue the life on the farm to help it become productive.
He, being a young farmer, knows well of these problems. I would like to ask him, and I would like to ask other members throughout the day as well, what things we in the national government Chamber could be doing to try to bring some excitement, purpose and vocation back to agriculture and farming in this country.
How do we bring youth back to agriculture in this country?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for such understanding of agriculture. Many may not know, but my colleague is a farmer. He shows a lot of interest in that area.
That is one of the biggest problems we have in Canadian agricultural communities today: the problem of youth and why youth will continue to farm in the conditions that their parents and their forefathers have farmed before.
My colleague is right when he says that it is difficult for young farmers to get into farming, or to stay in farming. My colleagues across the way know that, without the policies and the programs that governments provide because of the world situation in farming, many young people would not be eligible to farm.
There are a number of new ideas and new thoughts out there. I will give credit where credit is due. A lot of new ideas have come out with this Growing Together paper. A lot of people have got together.
All over the province of Ontario, too, different farm groups have got together to try to come up with new ideas to keep our youth in farming. We in the Liberal Party have formed a group to sit down to talk with farmers to develop these new ideas in new ways that will keep our youth in farming. Obviously, a lot of them have to do with providing the safety nets that are there in order to keep farmers on the land.
A lot of the problems with our youth in farming have to do with the fact that they cannot get proper funding. They deal with the same problems that all Canadians deal with: big businessmen and small businessmen in Canada, in trying to get access to proper funding to farm.
There have to be better ways for governments to signal to our young people that they will have stable supplies of money when they need it for many years down the line.
Unfortunately now, with the rises of interest rates and the volatility of our economic markets, those sorts of programs are not available. Those sorts of assurances to our young farmers are not available, so many of them are not getting into farming because, quite frankly, they do not have the security of moneys.
I thank my colleague for his question. I could go on an on, but I want to hear a question from the other side.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate being allowed a few minutes to consider this opposition motion and emphasize to the government, particularly at this critical time in the GATT negotiations, the need for the government to pursue with a good degree of vigour the fact that there are to be no new deals struck among the 96 or so countries that will be concluding the round of talks in Brussels in a few weeks. No new deals can be struck which will dismantle Canada's supply management programs.
Canadians face many tensions at this time in our history. We all find these very challenging. Sometimes we ask ourselves if anything at all is working any more. Well, I can tell you, Madam Speaker, some things still work and they work well. One of those things that is working well and has worked well for many years is

Canada's supply managed programs which work in the milk industry for milk, milk products, and works in the egg industry for eggs, egg products and poultry.
The result is that since 1970, approximately 20 years now, Canadians have enjoyed a good supply of high quality basic food products at a price that they can afford. No one is being exploited, neither the producer nor the consumer. The system has operated for 20 years with maximum efficiency and maximum effectiveness. It behoves the government of the day on behalf of all to see that no deals are struck at GATT which will see us turning back the clock on the basis on which these primary foods are produced and marketed in this country.
Let us look back and see what advances have been made in the dairy industry for example. We will soon realize the importance of having success in the present managed supply system. I know what used to happen in the dairy industry. The great fluctuations in prices brought people into the industry for short periods of time if prices were favourable, only to see them retreat out of the industry very quickly when prices fell below production costs.
No businessman in any other industry in this country could or would stay in business for very long if he could not count on a projected minimum price for his product, a price that had some relation to the cost of manufacturing the product. He would also want to be sure that there was going to be an ongoing need for his product.
The managed supply system was designed specifically to fill both those needs. A price which was based on production costs and a mechanism to ensure that the product would be needed. Canadians believe it is important for this country to be self-sufficient, particularly in dairy products.
A national survey conducted by Goldfarb Consultants, a reputable firm, in May of this year came up with some very interesting statistics as to the appreciation which Canadians have for dairy farmers and the way they operate.
It helps if you own the firm, doesn't it?

If you are basically honest, it doesn't really matter who owns it.
Supply
Two or three interesting statistics came out of that in summary, I suppose, of all the data that was collected. Seventy per cent of Canadians say that all milk products should be produced in Canada. Thirty-four per cent of Canadians said that they can come from other countries, but they want fresh milk. Some 85 per cent of Canadians thought that the dairy industry in Canada was in excellent shape and that dairy farmers were very efficient. Another interesting statistic is that 76 per cent of Canadians said that they would be willing to pay more for Canadian dairy products to support the Canadian dairy industry.
In summary of this report, the overwhelming majority of Canadians, 94 per cent, believe that it is important for the dairy industry in Canada to remain self-sufficient, without any outside interference from other countries.
Canadians can be supportive of the present marketing systems because they know that for 20 years they have had at their disposal a good supply of excellent products at a bargain price. Only 14 per cent to 17 per cent of disposable income of Canadians is spent on food. It is the lowest in the world when we consider the quality of our food and the fact that we live under some fairly harsh weather conditions which often affect the cost of production.
The target price for industrial milk, which is set by the Canadian Dairy Commission, has increased by only 4.7 per cent over the past four years from July 1986 to July 1990. The Consumer Price Index over the same period increased 19.3 per cent. This is possible because Canadian farmers are among the most efficient in the world and Canadian consumers are benefiting from that efficiency.
A Canadian family of four buys on the average two dozen eggs per week. At $1.50 a dozen, it will cost that family $156 a year for a highly nutritious food in which there is no waste. Eggs come for the most part in their own package and leave very little environmental burden on the community. How can we be so fortunate? It is because Canadian farmers are among the most efficient in the world, and they have become that way under managed marketing systems.
That is why the Canadian negotiators at GATT have to be tough minded when it comes to any tendency to barter away our production and marketing systems which

Supply
are working so well for the benefit of all Canadians, both producers and consumers.
Marketing boards have brought order and stability into one of Canada's most basic industries. Canadians who have benefited from these programs are urging the federal government to state unequivocally its commitment to the Canadian supply managed systems. A failure to do so would seriously compromise the trust placed by our farmers into the hands of those speaking on their behalf at the GATT negotiations. Canadians, both producers and consumers, will pay the price if we allow our managed marketing systems to be up for grabs.
I think my time is up by both clocks. I would be delighted to try and answer any questions.

Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague for his brilliant speech and his understanding of the Canadian farming situation.
Having a number of dairy farmers in his riding, he too has probably seen the number of editorials that have appeared in Canadian newspapers across Canada attacking our system of supply management, really attacking dairy farmers and calling them leeches on the system. I am wondering if the member would take this opportunity to give a short explanation to all Canadians of why our supply managed systems are so good and really tell Canadians that in fact they are not paying too much for their supply managed products.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the question from my colleague.
Another of my colleagues asked what the young farmer is looking for today. Any youth starting into the dairy industry today is looking for some stability, some future. You cannot have stability if you are living in a fluctuated market. My experience was that when the price of milk was high people jumped in, and then got out of the industry. How could he, for example, plan and buy a tractor which he needs in his industry and finance it over a period of years, as most of them have to do today and as we have all had to do? How could he possibly have that kind of faith when he can see absolutely no future stability in the industry?
Those who would criticize the Milk Marketing Board really do not understand how it works. The only time there is an increase from the man who has his $300,000, $400,000 or $500,000 investment is when there is an increase in his costs. If he wants to make a little more
money just so he will not stifle initiative, he can make more money if he becomes more efficient. That is why it is reflected in those few statistics I gave. The initiative is there to become very efficient. I think this would induce young people into the industry. There is some incentive, stability, and some reason for them to become efficient. They like the challenge, and I think they will come into the industry on that basis.
If we throw it to the wolves as it used to be when the price was up and down and depend on another country, can we imagine a country like Canada depending on a neighbour, even with the best of intentions, to supply some of our basic foods? What a disgrace that would be.
I am using the Milk Marketing Board as an example. I think we have the largest egg producer in North America in my riding. The same applies to the egg industry also. There is a good supply. The quality is excellent and the price is right.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to rise and speak to this motion before the House today.
The member for Haldimand-Norfolk is asking this House, through the GATT negotiations and in over-all economic policies, to recognize the vital and valuable role farmers play in maintaining the Canadian way of life.
I would suggest that this government's record stands as proof that the well-being of Canadian farmers has been a priority in the past and will continue to be a priority in the future.
Between 1984 and 1989, direct and indirect federal expenditures in agriculture totalled almost $22 billion. Again, in 1990, we have undertaken various initiatives, including $500 million in direct cash payments to help with the cash flow assistance. Also, we are providing an interest relief program of up to $95 million for this current crop year for grains and oilseeds producers.
That kind of support for farmers is unprecedented in Canadian history. That kind of support clearly shows our commitment to farmers and our recognition of the importance of maintaining that Canadian way of life we speak of. Our commitment goes beyond dollars and cents. While we have willingly used the federal Treasury to offset farm income problems, we have also undertak-

en two major initiatives to ensure the long-term well-being of the Canadian agricultural sector.
Domestically we are in the midst of a major agrifood policy review. It has brought all the partners in the agrifood sector together to define policy options that will ensure this $50 billion industry can keep pace in this rapidly changing world.
Through that policy review, we are looking at ways to ensure the industry is market responsive, self-reliant, regionally sensitive, and environmentally sustainable. Those four pillars, as they are known, are the foundation of a healthy and durable agrifood industry.
As part of the review, a govemment/industry task force has designed a new safety net system that will give farmers predictability and stability over the long term. This will help to address some of the concerns that the previous speakers have been raising in their speeches. Such a system will allow us to get away from the ad hoc kind of assistance we have had to provide in recent years, ad hoc assistance that has treated the symptoms and not the problem. It is difficult to farm in that type of environment when one cannot predict into the long term. We believe that the safety nets that are being put forward will assist in giving it that stability that is required.
It is hoped that these new safety nets will be in place for the grains and oilseeds sector for the next crop year. If there is a willingness of all members of this House of Commons to put that system into place for the 1991 crop year, I believe we can get that work done and I believe we have an obligation to do that.
It is also hoped that the next crop year will find us well on our way to a fair and equitable world trade environment. It is most important as well that we deal with that world trade environment. To that end, Canada has played a major role in having agriculture included in the Uruguay round of the General Agreement on Thriffs and Trade.
This initiative at the international level is also crucial to the long-term well-being of our agrifood sector. We need a new world trading order in agriculture if we are to get away from the foolish subsidy battles that have hurt
Supply
our grains and oilseeds sector so badly. We need a new world trading order that will allow our supply management sectors to operate under clearly defined rules. We need a new world trading order if our rural communities are to grow and to prosper.
The Uruguay round is scheduled to end in December, and Canada has firmly stated its goals in these negotiations. In particular, we are seeking the elimination of export subsidies, a substantial reduction in internal subsidies, improved market access, greater security for supply management through a clarified and strengthened Article XI, and development of rules on health and sanitary measures so they are not misused as disguised barriers to trade, which is so often the case today.
Our offer which we tabled in Geneva on October 15 was developed in close consultation with the agrifood industry and the provincial governments. In fact industry leaders have widely praised our offer.
Jim Caldwell of the Canadian Cattlemen's Association had this to say about it:
It is a well-balanced package. If other countries would agree, it
would be a good start.
Albert Chambers of the Canadian Chicken Marketing Agency said:
It's what we expected. Poultry and egg producers would have little
or nothing to complain about.
We believe that we have developed a balanced position in these negotiations: an approach that reflects the fact our agrifood industry is both domestically oriented and also export oriented. If we can bring about an end to the destructive use of export subsidies, Canadian farmers will be able to compete fairly against other farmers and not the treasuries of other governments. If we can get Article XI strengthened and clarified, our farmers can operate supply management programs secure in the knowledge that they are complying with internationally accepted rules.
Clearly a successful agreement on agriculture in the Uruguay round must be of benefit to all Canadian agriculture. We cannot pick and choose. It has to be of benefit to all of the agricultural sector.
As the December deadline for the Uruguay round approaches, we plan to continue our close consultation with the industry. We want what is best for the industry,

November 2, 1990
Supply
and that means a world trade environment that is fair and equitable.
We are disappointed that the Europeans have yet to table their offer. We are extremely disappointed that both the Europeans and the Americans have upped their use of export subsidies. Hopefully both are only flexing their muscles as we head toward the crucial stage of the negotiations.
Canada is committed to seeing this trade war brought to an end. We can only hope that other trading nations share in that commitment.
A successful end to the Uruguay round will help to ensure a bright future for our agrifood sector. This in turn will ensure a bright future for our over-all economy. After all, we cannot forget that our agrifood sector is responsible for about 10 per cent of our gross domestic product and employs more than 14 per cent of Canadians.
This government recognizes the importance of this industry. That is why we are doing our best to ensure the Uruguay round is successful. That is why we are in the midst of a major domestic agrifood policy review. We want to ensure this industry has a stable and predictable future. We want to ensure this industry can grow and prosper, because as this industry grows and prospers, so does Canada.
I hope, with the various speeches from the different parties that will be given in this House, we can come up with some very positive, workable solutions because we know how important the agrifood sector is to this great nation of Canada. It has developed this country in the early production of food.
We have the ability to produce much beyond our domestic requirements and we know that much of the world requires food. We also know that many countries of the world which require that food have an inability to pay. We have to work out some solutions in order to keep a strong viable agriculture sector, while keeping in mind that there are others in this world who are not as fortunate as we are.
I hope when members are turning their thoughts toward agriculture in this country that they keep that in mind. By working together, as we did with our Growing Together task force paper, we will bring together not only the politicians but governments at all levels. It will affect trade in all sectors, right to the grassroots. People were
talking about the well-being of the agrifood sector and their representatives resulting in wonderful co-operation and excellent consultations. We believe that we are developing, not only at GATT, but in this country, a better understanding among all the players. By doing that, everyone will prosper because if agriculture prospers in this country, all of us will prosper.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to salute the member for Huron- Bruce. Many of us realize that he is a farmer and he has accomplished a lot in this sector over the years.
I would like to come back to the question that I asked my colleague. He knows that we are at the crossroads right now in this very important sector. He has spent many years and has enjoyed and inspired many others to get involved in this sector. What does he think we should be doing to create the excitement and interest for young people to work and live on farms and for those who have money to invest in farms?
Five or six years ago in this House, if one asked someone if they would be interested in going into environmental studies, 9 out of 10 of our youth would run the other way. They did not recognize the importance of the environment.
Tbday we have a sector, agriculture, that is going to be feeding the world over the next 10 to 15 years. For some unknown reason we cannot seem to get our youth turned on and interested in making the commitment to the vocation of farming. I stress vocation because it really is not like an office tower job on Bay Street or St. Catherines Street where one works nine to five. It is a full and total commitment.
What I would like to hear from this member, who has owned and operated a farm successfully most of his life, are his thoughts as to what we should be doing to bring youth back to farming?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question. It does give us the option to address a particular issue which concerns all of us. It is not a new concern. This is something that has happened over a number of years. All of us in this House who represent rural ridings ask many times how a young person can enter into the farm sector.
There is a new generation of farmers approaching. There is also a generation that is already there. That does not mean there are still not difficult challenges that they must face. These have been difficult and we must

recognize that. Farm incomes have been low and expenses have been high. Many of these people have trimmed their costs to the bare bones as much as possible. Very often they have not had adequate support from their operations to give them the type of living that some other people in the country have and enjoy. We have to start with the problem, and the problem is that there has not been the stability that is required in agriculture. We know ad hoc programs will get one through for today and for a short period but not in the long term. We believe with the Growing Together paper and the work that is evolving from that paper, particularly that which will address the farm finance sector, that we need long-term, predictable programs, such as the safety nets that would be of assistance in making that commitment to the future of agriculture.
I do believe there are many young people in this country who would love to enter into the vocation of farming either on the family farm or young people who are new entrants. We know that at agricultural colleges the enrolment is maintained, and that there is an interest in the agrifood business and so we believe the will is still there. With the safety nets, before one plants a crop one can predict what one's income will be for that year. That makes the borrower feel comfortable and it also makes the lender feel more comfortable. Perhaps a preferred rate could be established if everybody feels comfortable in this situation. That is one of the first steps toward some of the stability that is really needed.
We also have been unable to predict the grains and oilseeds sector because of the lack of a world agreement. I am sure everyone has witnessed what has happened over the last number of years. In 1989, the grain producing nations of the world transferred something like $245 billion U.S. to the farm sector. It is embarrassing when we think of what that is doing; and still, a third of the people in this world are going to bed hungry every night. That is something we have to address as well.
Tb come back to the hon. member's question, I believe that more young people will go into agriculture if we put the right policies in place. We have a task force on farm financing which is addressing new entrants to agriculture, not only youth but new entrants, which I believe is important. If we can come out with the proper programs, that will help.

There has always been a problem, for as long as I have farmed and that is all my life, of intergenerational transfer of land from one generation to the next. So if we can address that issue, without having to refinance the farm every generation, that would help us greatly as well. But the most important thing is that income should be predictable and be at a level that gives an opportunity for a reasonable living. This would be the most encouraging thing we could have happen for our young people.

Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to contribute a few comments to this debate on agriculture. Like you, Madam Speaker, I am very concerned about what is happening at the current GATT talks.
We will have to wait until the end of these talks to find out what the impact of agreements will be on Quebec producers, for instance, who share the same type of prosperous farming area, and we hope that will remain so.
For the benefit of hon. members, I want to say that thousands of farmers have written to us to express their concerns. I think it is absolutely vital, especially during this debate, to ensure that hon. members are aware of the legitimate demands of Quebec producers, demands that are summed up in three short paragraphs, Madam Speaker. First, it is clear that properly maintained and operated supply management systems, particularly as they apply to dairy, poultry and egg producers, are essential if we are to maintain balanced production and a measure of security for our farmers.
Of course, we cannot have a management system if we cannot control imports, and obviously, if import controls are replaced by a customs tariff, this would lead to a gradual dismantling of our supply management system.
Finally, Quebec producers are anxious to see their price and income stabilization programs maintained in their present form. As you know, Quebec has a program that is probably the most generous and best adapted to the present situation in agriculture, which means that maintaining crop insurance and farm credit programs must be one of the priorities at the current GATT talks. As we see it, these programs do not cause any distortion in production and marketing.

November 2, 1990
Supply
While the talks are taking place in Geneva, many fanners are very worried. They have substantial investments that are on the line, and the banks are getting nervous. I therefore hope the government will never consider signing an agreement that does not respect existing rights.
I am sure the parliamentary secretary, who is very well informed on this issue, is prepared to give us the assurance that the vested rights of Canadian farmers will not be tampered with.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for giving me the opportunity to once again state our position and support for Article XI which is the basis of our supply management sector, whether it is dairy or poultry.
We tabled our position after consulting fully with both of those industries. We have not wavered in any way from the position that was developed by those two sectors and we will maintain our position. We have no intention of moving from that position.
We have met constantly with the dairy producers and the poultry sector and their support has been very valuable to us in developing the position and maintaining it. It is very clear to the government that that is what we would like to have.
Madam Speaker, I wonder if it would be permissible if I could go back to the hon. member who was talking about young farmers.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will have to interrupt the hon. member. The period for questions and comments has now expired. However, I would be quite prepared, if it is the pleasure of the House, to allow the parliamentary secretary to answer the questions.
Agreed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I thank you, Madam Speaker, and the House for that co-operation. I just want to say that the age distribution of farmers has been fairly constant since 1931. The proportion of farmers who were under 35 was actually higher in 1986 than in any census year between 1961 and 1976.
Also between 1981 and 1986, just over 28,000 individuals under the age of 35 started new farm businesses. I just thought the House would be interested in those statistics.

Madam Speaker, I thank the parliamentary secretary for his comments. He knows, as I said, that I believe the papers are going in the right direction and we need more consultations with farmers. Quite frankly, farmers are asking whether or not the money is going to be there to back up all the promises that are coming out of these consultations.
The member is quite aware of what his colleague, the Minister for International Trade said in this House on October 15, as reported at page 14143 of Hansard:
The Minister of Agriculture should be ashamed at the amount of
assistance he is giving Canadian fanners.
I want to give the parliamentary secretary an opportunity to stand in this House today and to refute those statements, and to tell all Canadian farmers that in fact once all the consultations are finished, once all the programs are there and made available, that the money will be there to provide for these programs.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would just like to state again that this government has been committed to agriculture ever since we took over the governing of this country in 1984. The programs we brought forward and the assistance we have given has been consistent and has always been there when the need was there. That will continue to be there as well.
Regardless of what the future holds, we believe that if we have proper negotiations, it will not require as many tax dollars to assist if we can bring some common sense to the world marketplace.
But I do say, and I will say again, that we will be there to support our agriculture sectors as we have in the past.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It being eleven o'clock, pursuant to Standing Order 30(5), the House will now proceed to Statements by Members pursuant to Standing Order 31.

Yesterday, Madam Speaker, the minister responsible for regional development, the hon. Benoit Bouchard, was in Bona-venture in the riding of my colleague Darryl Gray where he announced the federal government's participation in the Atlantic salmon enhancement program in Quebec.
Under this joint federal-provincial agreement the Government of Canada contributes $12 million towards a program to restock Atlantic salmon rivers and develop sports fishing.
Madam Speaker, allow me to welcome this federal government initiative and pay tribute to the Quebec Federation of Atlantic Salmon. For a number of years now it has been playing a leading role in the preparation of this program, and it will continue to ensure that it is properly implemented.

Madam Speaker, Canadians will know that the government since 1984 has increased taxation 32 times. If the goods and services tax were to be implemented, it would be number 33.
The government has shown an immense creativity in raising taxes, but there is a type of tax that we are not talking a great deal about and that is fee for service or charge-back for certain services. For example, there is a new twist now, charging employees for certain particular services.
Here is one example. There is a new parking policy which now requires employees to pay, and pay a lot, at the Winnipeg Taxation Centre. The parking facility there is really quite inadequate. There are not enough parking plugs and they have been requested over a year ago. Of course there are severe winter conditions there and if anyone doubts that I would invite them to come and pay a visit. These plugs were requested last year. To date nothing has been done. There are not enough spaces for
employees. The centre is not centrally located, there is poor bus service, and no viable alternative for parking.
Apparently this is taking place in a number of cities across Canada and in a number of areas of government, not only at the Winnipeg Taxation Centre.

When will the government stop overtaxing Canadians? And when will it treat employees with fairness?

Madam Speaker, the residents of the riding of Saint-Maurice enthusiastically welcome the Prime Minister's announcement concerning the future of our country, and they intend to participate actively in this great national debate. We will remind our friends in English Canada that Quebec is a distinct society, a fact that will have to be recognized once and for all.
Unlike members of the Bloc quebecois, most Quebec members will answer the Prime Minister's call. Our friends in the Bloc quebecois should also make a positive contribution to this endeavour, if only because the interest of Quebecers-as long as they remain Canadians-is that the systems works.
My message to the member for Shefford and the member for Richelieu is that the role of members in the Canadian Parliament is to seek formulas likely to improve the country, not to plan sterile strategies to destroy it.

Madam Speaker, according to a report published in The Ottawa Citizen this week, the National Capital Commission seems ready to make some recommendations concerning the Daly Building.
In the past years the project has inspired heated debate on its heritage value and the viability of preserving it without major modifications despite its unsafe structure. Anyone walking by the south side of the building along Rideau Street can see that this eyesore's

zero set-back makes any work being done around it dangerous and inconvenient.
There can be nothing gained in keeping the south side of the building intact. I call upon the NCC to heed the advice of experts presently involved in the project, to remove the dangerously substandard stones, to move the building much further away from the street, and to produce a replica of the original Chicago-style building constructed in 1905. All of this will thereby properly enhance the streetscape at the bottleneck of Confederation Square.

Madam Speaker, as grain stocks in western Canada mount and world fuel prices rise due to the situation in the Middle East, it seems timely to consider the economic viability of increasing the production of ethanol, a gas extender produced by the fermentation of biomass feedstocks such as low quality grains.
Contained in the report of the Standing Committee of the Environment of October of this year is a recommendation which states: "Canadian energy policy-making must have as its most immediate focus the more efficient and conserving use of energy."
Ethanol blended fuels offer a wide range of advantages to the motor fuel producer, the marketer, the consumer, and the public at large. Ethanol is capable of dramatically reducing dependence on foreign oil and boosting our farm economy.
I urge fuel producers and the government to give serious consideration to the increasing of our production-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret, but the time of the hon. member has expired.

Madam Speaker, considering the way it handled the Hibernia project and its opposition to the principle of anti-scab legislation proposed by a former Tory, the hon. member for Richelieu, this government has abandoned Quebec and Canadian workers. The irony and hypocrisy of it all! Francophone Tory members who don't even have the balls to defend the real interests of Quebecers!
I went to the Levis-Lauzon shipyards and I heard and echoed the alarm sounded by Robert Monette, president of the union local at MIL Davie. The government had clearly missed the boat on the Hibernia project, and then we saw Tbry masks drop a few days after Halloween, when they objected to the principle of anti-scab legislation. Today, we see the true face of these Tories, Madam Speaker, a face that is anti-union, anti-worker and anti-Quebec.

Madam Speaker, today, the media reported that Quebec Minister Gil Remillard was not satisfied with the federal government's contribution to regional development in Quebec.
The progress report for the 1988 Canada-Quebec agreement on regional economic development, dated September 30, 1990, contains the following information: In the resource regions, the federal government introduced programs with a total of $214.99 million, 75.9 per cent of the $283 million provided for these regions. Of that amount, 23.6 per cent or $66.91 million has already been committed, while the province has invested only $98.66 million, 48.6 per cent of a total of $203 million. Madam Speaker, only 2.6 per cent of this amount or $5.6 million has been committed.
In the central regions, the federal government has already committed $43.75 million, as opposed to the province's $3.52 millions.
Madam Speaker, Minister Remillard's eloquence does not extend to figures, so I think he should learn quickly to give credit where credit is due, for the benefit of Quebecers.

Madam Speaker, for the last two years, Prince Edward Island has suffered at the hands of Canada Post. We have seen closures of

rural post offices, reduction in services, and most recently the cancellation of Saturday rural mail delivery.
It has reached the point that a two-tiered system is developing in types of services provided by the corporation. My constituents who live in rural route areas have discovered that not only are they deprived of Saturday rural delivery, but they cannot even pick up their mail from the post office on Saturdays.
Islanders deserve better treatment from Canada Post and the opportunity to voice their dissatisfaction with recent actions taken by the corporation. I urge the minister responsible for Canada Post to respond to my previous request that a committee be struck to examine the recent cuts and discrepancies in the corporation's activities in Prince Edward Island.

Madam Speaker, we must continue our efforts to heighten public awareness and renew our joint commitment to improving the reading and writing skills of Canadian men and women.
According to a recent survey of literacy levels in Canada by Statistics Canada, 38 per cent of Canadian adults lack basic routine reading and mathematical skills.
International Literacy Year has provided opportunities for action, and people have become more aware of the problem. A special effort has been made to raise the literacy levels of Canadian men and women. However, we must not stop there. For 4.5 million Canadians, reading and writing is a daily recurring problem.
Madam Speaker, we cannot let all this human potential go to waste because of lack of skills. Our own development is at stake, both as individuals and as a nation.

Madam Speaker, the Fraser River is over 1,200 kilometres long and drains over 230,000 square kilometres of
British Columbia. It is a vital part of the provincial ecosystem.
The lower Fraser is fortunate to have the Fraser River estuary management program to monitor the environmental health of the river as it empties into the lower mainland estuary. No such agency exists to provide a clear and effective plan to safeguard the future of the upper Fraser.
The upper Fraser requires a plan and a process to permit a better balance of economic and environmental considerations, as well as a framework for effective research and monitoring programs. We need to develop an integrated strategy to clean up the entire Fraser River and address critical issues such as water quality and the impact on the upper Fraser of industrial, forestry, and agricultural practices.
An upper Fraser management program could and should provide all agencies and non-governmental organizations interested in the Fraser River, an opportunity for input.
If the government is truly interested in-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member's time has now expired. The hon. member for Portage-Interlake.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to speak about a subject that is of importance to all Canadians.
Our children-the children of Canada and, indeed, the children of the earth-need our protection, our support, and our love.
I congratulate our Prime Minister for his efforts at the historic World Summit on Children at the United Nations. This hallmark event has raised children's rights to new heights and expectations.
I would like to thank the many persons in my constituency of Portage-Interlake who continue to drop off at my constituency office donations of children's necessities and cash to be donated to the many orphanages in the country of Romania. Their generosity will help these children and will not be forgotten.

November 2, 1990
Finally, I wish to welcome to this world one new Canadian, Cali Beryl Blank, the bouncing new daughter of Sheldon and Irene Blank of Winnipeg. May she grow up to know a better world for children than exists today.

Madam Speaker, yesterday the Minister of State for Privatization announced that he was seeking bids for the purchase of the shares of Nordion Inc., a subsidiary of Canada Development Investment Corporation.
The government is in danger of developing a bad habit for cutting bad backroom deals. The sale of Route Canada by CN was just one example of this. In this time of economic uncertainty, concrete steps must be taken to protect taxpayers and employees from unscrupulous purchasers dedicated to an asset strip of Nordion.
I urge the minister responsible to make public his ministry's current market appraisal of Nordion, as well as all bids submitted and not withdrawn, the agreement of purchase and sale, and the remuneration agreement with Wood Gundy, which is the bid manager, so that Canadians are not kept in the dark as this Crown corporation goes on the chopping block.

Madam Speaker, I want to assure the House and the people interested in the Parrsboro Fossil Museum that the federal commitment to fund the museum is in place and confirmed. As well, I am pleased to report that Hon. Ron Giffin, Minister of Education for the Province of Nova Scotia, has confirmed the commitment of the province. Further, the private investor has committed to go ahead with the project as soon as possible.
Funding for the museum resulted from a unique agreement by several departments and levels of government and was only made possible by the participation of the private sector partner.
Although some opportunistic individuals have tried to create some negative publicity about the museum, we are all determined to succeed in this genuine historic project in an area of high unemployment. It will be the corner-stone of an economic turnaround for the area and the community is solidly behind the geological society in a very positive way.

I rise today to underline the fundamental importance of having representatives from Canada's northern territories on the recently formed Citizens' Forum on Canada's Future panel.
Surely, if we are to engage in a process of national renewal, it is essential that all regions of the country have a voice. I need not remind the House that the Yukon and Northwest Territories encompass one third of Canada's land mass. The Yukon and Northwest Territories were left out of the Meech Lake process.
The Prime Minister spoke yesterday of consultation from coast to coast. Well, I want to call on the Prime Minister for consultation from coast to coast to coast. I call on the Prime Minister today not to ignore the reality of Canada, to acknowledge Canada's majestic north, and to give the message to Canadians in the north that our views count and that our voice should be heard.
I call on the Prime Minister to ask for nominations from the Yukon and Northwest Territories to serve on this very important panel on national unity.

Madam Speaker, Article 19 is an international London based anti-censorship monitoring organization. It has said recently that Canada's protection of freedom of information is too weak. The group in its report to the United Nations Human Rights Commission urged that federal budget cuts in programs to promote the use of aboriginal languages be reconsidered. During the recent Oka crisis, the news media's freedoms were severely diminished.
I would hope that the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs in its consideration of the events of this past

summer at Kanesatake would take these and other words of censure from the international community into account.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have questions today for the Minister of the Environment on his handling of the Rafferty-Alameda dam project and what it says about his commitment and that of the government to having a sound environment for all Canadians.
Yesterday an affidavit was tabled in the Saskatchewan Court of Queen's Bench, sworn under oath by Premier Devine of Saskatchewan, in which the premier said that on September 5 he met with the minister in the minister's office and he and the minister agreed that the dam project would go ahead and there would be no environmental assessment completed until after the dams were completed. Yet the minister in this House on October 12 said and I quote: "There was no such agreement".
How could the minister tell the House that there was no such agreement when the premier of Saskatchewan swore under oath in an affidavit tabled in the Saskatchewan court that there was such an agreement and that he and the minister even shook hands on it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, first of all I would like to repeat for my hon. colleague that my position in this case has always been very straightforward. It has been to say that I wanted the process of a full review to be completed. There were documents that were filed late Wednesday afternoon in Saskatchewan before the court. I asked the court, through our legal counsel, to give me the time to respond to those documents. I intend to do so. I can also say that I maintain the position that I took before my colleagues in this House on October 12, saying that there was no such agreement.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have the premier's affidavit right here in my
Oral Questions
hand. In it the premier swears under oath that the minister made an agreement with him, which was repeated before officials at a luncheon, that the dam project could go ahead and there would be no assessment until the project was completed.
Will the minister swear his own affidavit under oath, setting out what he said here, and will he go to Saskatchewan immediately to allow himself to be cross-examined under oath about his affidavit?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I just said very clearly in my answer to the first question that the documents had been tabled before the bench very late Wednesday afternoon. We asked for an adjournment so that I would be in a position to provide the equivalent documents on the federal government's position, and I will do that. Those documents will be sworn and they will be deposited before the court this afternoon.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if the minister and the government are fully committed to having an environmental review before the project goes ahead and if they want the court to prevent the project from going ahead before this has happened, why has the government, through its lawyers, asked the court for another six days delay before the case is heard?
I am told that earth moving equipment is working on the dam day and night, seven days a week. Even though the minister wants to file his own affidavit, why can the case not begin right now with the material that is already available? Does it not mean that the minister is not serious if the minister, through his lawyers, wants another six days before the case even begins to be heard?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is very simple. I have mentioned that twice now. I will mention it a third time to make sure that my hon. colleague opposite understands it.
The Government of Saskatchewan made available new materials to the court on Wednesday afternoon, roughly at four o'clock local time. We were advised of this new material. I think that it is only appropriate that on our side we have the opportunity to file equivalent material so that the court can reach a full and knowledgeable decision. That is what we are doing.

November 2, 1990
Oral Questions

Madam Speaker, in the affidavit filed by the president of SaskPower, Mr. George Hill, it is alleged that the minister stated that if the Rafferty Environmental Review Panel quit, "So be it".
Did the minister say, and I quote from the affidavit, "If in fact, it did quit, it would probably increase this minister's options". Did the minister say "he did not care" one way or the other.
Is there any limit to this minister's or this government's cynicism. Having said these things, does the minister believe that he will ever again be able to regain the credibility which is required to be the ultimate defender of the nation's environment?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will repeat again, it is very clear. I want the process to be completed. That is why we have undertaken the moves that we are undertaking. I will be making a full declaration before the court in the form of an affidavit that will be tabled this afternoon.
Other than that, because the case is before the courts, I have no further answers to give.

Madam Speaker, that is a cop-out, and the minister knows it.
Did the minister say to the premier of Saskatchewan that he should not communicate with this minister through his ministerial office because the minister cannot handle his own bureaucrats?
As a result, was subsequent correspondence between this minister and the premier of Saskatchewan not carried on through the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister? Was the Chief of Staff of the Prime Minister involved in this whole scene, as is alleged?
Is the Minister of the Environment, by his denials, not only impugning his own credibility, but impugning the credibility of his department? And now, is he not impugning the credibility of the office of the Prime Minister? Who, in heaven's name, are the Canadian people to believe?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is very clear: There was no agreement reached on September 5. We are before the courts. The affidavit will be filed this afternoon, and affidavits
from many of the people that my hon. colleague has mentioned.
There was no agreement and we want the process respected. We want a full environmental review of the project before work is allowed to continue, pursuant to the only agreement that was ever signed between Canada and Saskatchewan which is the January 26, 1990, agreement.

Madam Speaker, in the issue of the Rafferty-Alameda dam, what is at stake here is the credibility of this minister and government, the implications for future projects and the seriousness of this government to have a real environmental review process.
Hear, hear.

For that reason, Madam Speaker, I believe the Minister of the Environment must clarify his actions for this House.
In the affidavit put forward by Premier Devine, he says that the hon. member for Souris-Moose Mountain, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister, was aware of a deal that had been made.
I ask the Minister of the Environment, would the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister not have advised him on September 5 of this deal? Would the Principal Secretary of the Prime Minister not have advised him? Who is in charge here? Is the Minister of the Environment in charge? Can we trust him?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, it is quite clear. The meeting that was held on September 5 was attended by myself, people from Saskatchewan, some of my officials and some of my political staff. There was no agreement. I have made that very clear to this House. I repeat it right now.

A supplementary, Madam Speaker, for the Minister of the Environment. Clearly, there are two stories here. Rather than argue about the stories, the minister says he is going to file his own statement, I want to ask the minister about another matter.
The environmental review process to which he is said he is very committed to is very important to all Canadians in his implications for James Bay and his implications for other megaprojects.

The Minister of the Environment said the panel quit because they felt they could not work under the circumstances of the dam proceeding. I ask the Minister of the Environment if he has given consideration to appointing another panel. If so, who will be on that panel? Who has agreed to sit on that environmental panel?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, given that the purpose of this exercise is to ensure that we have a process that is carried out fully, certainly the answer to the question of whether or not I am looking at the appointment of another panel is yes, obviously, because that is the only way the process can be allowed to be completed.
I would also like to suggest to the hon. member opposite that, given that we have a guidelines order but no legislation to ensure that all major projects in this country are fully assessed from an environmental point of view before construction begins, I would certainly urge her party to support strongly Bill C-78, which is now before committee.
Madam Speaker, a supplementary question. The minister well knows that there are more loopholes and more exemptions allowed under Bill C-78 than even under the current system.
Hear, hear.

Madam Speaker, the Minister of the Environment says he is going to appoint a panel. We have construction continuing 24 hours a day. The project is continuing and the minister has asked for a further delay of six days. When is the Minister of the Environment going to appoint another panel? What is the date? Who has agreed to sit on this panel to review this project?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the whole purpose of our being in court is to seek an injunction so that the work will cease on the project at the moment and that will allow us, at that point, to appoint the new panel and to move along with the respect that we have, as a government, for the process of environmental review in this country.

Madam Speaker, my question is to the Acting Prime Minister. It concerns
Oral Questions
the credibility of not only the Minister of the Environment but the whole government on this particular issue.
We have the sworn affidavit from the premier of the province of Saskatchewan who states, and I quote: "He", that is the federal Minister of the Environment, "invited me to shake hands on the agreement we had made, which we did". He further states, under oath, that the agreement was communicated not only to the member of Parliament for Souris-Moose Mountain but also to the Chief of Staff of the Prime Minister on that same day.
Now we have the Minister of the Environment, in the House, claiming no deal was made, and the premier of Saskatchewan stating that not only was a deal struck, it was communicated to the Chief of Staff of the Prime Minister. My question to the Acting Prime Minister is who is lying, the Minister of the Environment or the premier of Saskatchewan? Who is lying?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member may want to rephrase her question.
I will rephrase it then, Madam Speaker. My question to the Acting Prime Minister is who is not telling the truth?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, there was a meeting on September 5. We did discuss a number of issues. There was no agreement made to change the agreement that was signed on January 26, 1990. That is still the agreement that is in force. We want that agreement to be respected so that environmental concerns in this country can be met.

Madam Speaker, the minister is making a very serious allegation, that the premier of Saskatchewan was lying under oath. The Minister of the Environment continues to state that no such agreement was reached when, in fact, we have a sworn affidavit from the premier of Saskatchewan who states that not only was an agreement-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Will the hon. member put her question, please.

My question is for the Acting Prime Minister. If there is anybody on the government side of the House who cares about the environment, will they tell us who is telling the truth on this particular issue, the

November 2, 1990
Oral Questions
premier of Saskatchewan or the Minister of the Environment?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member knows the rules of the House better than her questions would suggest she does. She knows what language is unparliamentary. Also she has always had a very keen eye for language that might make the television news. She should subvert her interest in the television news to her interest in this parliamentary process.
The answer has been provided by the Minister of the Environment. There will be affidavits filed later in the day on behalf of the Government of Canada that will make the position of the Government of Canada very clear on the matter. She should not try to seize a momentary deadline because of the natural timetables that are involved in a court process.

Madam Speaker, Manitobans cannot be and are not indifferent to what is going on in Saskatchewan. Manitobans are deeply concerned about what the Rafferty-Alameda dam project might do to water quality and water quantity in the Souris River on the Manitoba side of the border.
However, the environmental review panel has resigned; it is gone. Without the review panel in place, how does the Minister of the Environment plan to proceed with an assessment of any impact on the environment in Manitoba?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, that is the reason we are encouraged. We are encouraged because we want the agreement of January 26, 1990 respected. The reason that we are encouraged is also because the panel resigned once it found out that that agreement was not being respected.
Depending on the court's decision, then we would move very expeditiously to appoint a new panel to make sure that the work is completed and that the process of environmental review is fully respected in this instance.

Madam Speaker, I am sure the Manitobans will want the minister to keep his promise on that.
The Rafferty-Alameda project was preceded by an agreement with the Americans. Canada promised to build the dam, to build it very quickly, and in return the Americans promised to kick in $41 million.
Now the federal government has lost control over the project. Besides, the agreement was signed before the environmental impact assessment.
Are we not headed for a possible international mess with the Americans and all because of the negligence of this government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it became painfully apparent by late September-early October that the agreement which had been signed between Saskatchewan and Canada under the court order that had been issued for environmental assessment was not being respected.
We immediately moved to seek an injunction in court, and that is what we are proceeding to do, again to ensure that a full process of environmental review be conducted on the project according to the court order that was handed down back in December 1989.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the same minister.
Today is November 2. According to the affidavit, on September 5, on September 17, on September 28, on October 5, and again on October 10, the Saskatchewan government let the federal government know-either the minister himself, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister or the chief of staff of the Prime Minister-what its position was.
Why did the alarm bells not ring? Why did the federal government not have a position to defend the environment? Why was nothing done to defend the federal government position?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I just want to tell my hon. colleague that throughout that period there were ongoing discussions between the Government of Saskatchewan and myself to try to reach an agreement that would allow the panel and the process to be followed throughout.
Those conversations took place throughout September and early October. The last conversation was held the day when we had unfortunately to recognize that no accommodation could be reached, that the panel had

resigned, and that we had to take hard action, namely seek an injunction in court.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister.
If the minister were aware-and he must have been after all those days of communications-that there was such a problem, why was nothing made public? Why was the public kept in the dark? Why were others not in a position to know that the environment was being threatened? Why were others not told that the Saskatchewan government believed it had a deal? Why was everything kept in the dark? Why was everything kept a secret? Why was the public not able to defend the environment, like this minister has refused to do?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, throughout this period the panel was going about its job according to its terms of reference to fulfil an environmental process which we feel is very important for Canadians and for people throughout the country. That panel was working and that work was advancing.
During that time we were trying to discuss with Saskatchewan some of the controversy that had emerged over the last six months. The work was being done and was proceeding.
We would like very much to be able to assure right now that that process be maintained and that work be completed.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of the Environment.
He will know that in paragraph 84 of the affidavit of George Hill he states: "When the meal was concluded, which would have been around 1.35, the minister asked the premier if there was anything further, and when the premier replied that there was not, the hon. Robert de Cotret invited the premier to shake hands on the deal which they had made, and the two of them so shook hands."
For the benefit of all Canadians, would the Minister of the Environment explain why he now denies that there was a secret deal with regard to this matter?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the member is quoting from the affidavit. The case is before the courts. I have indicated clearly to this House that I will be responding on behalf of the Government of Canada to these affidavits by an affidavit of my own this afternoon.
I would only hope that this matter can be resolved by the courts and not resolved in this kind of public discussion.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister.
I have an affidavit signed by the premier of Saskatchewan. Paragraph 18 reads in part: "On September 5,1990 he telephoned and spoke with the honourable Len Gustafson, MP". He goes on to say, and I have the full extract here for the Acting Prime Minister: "I also kept my appointment with the chief of staff of the Prime Minister and I advised him of the agreement and the terms thereof. He informed me that he was pleased it was all behind us."
Would the Acting Prime Minister clarify the matter for all Canadians and admit to Canadians and to the House that there was a secret back room deal on this project?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I congratulate the Whip on his appointment and on his enthusiasm. It is too bad that his facts are not consistent with his rhetoric.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: You're calling the premier a liar?

speechtext:

As my colleague, the Minister of the Environment has said, there was no deal. As he also said, there will be further affidavits filed this afternoon. Rather than seeking Andy Warhol's 15 seconds of fame on television at noon, the hon. member should let the court process carry forward.
