speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister.
The terms of reference of the Spicer Commission are not clear, not by a long shot. Canadians have many questions concerning either the make-up of the commission or its work mandate.
I should like to ask the Acting Prime Minister whether the Spicer Commission will be a substitute for the promise made by the government or the Prime Minister to appoint a national commission on native peoples affairs? And are we to infer that the Spicer Commission will replace or defer another government promise that Parliament will address the reform of this institution and this country, beginning with the Senate? Can we expect an early start on Senate reform?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we hope to see a reform in current Senate practices, and Canada would be well served if the Liberal senators were to drop their tactics aimed at stalling the proceedings of the Senate.
But of course the government and Parliament will have to take other measures to reform our institutions, not only the Senate but the Commons as well where changes are necessary, as they are with respect to other federal-provincial and Canadian practices.
We believe that such a great national debate should not be the exclusive preserve of parliamentarians. As MPs we do have a role to play, but then so do all Canadians. Given yesterday's announcement about the establishment of the Spicer Commission, the Canadian government is now in a good position to participate fully in the decision-making process involving the future of this country.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Spicer task force may be good group therapy for the majority, but many of us in this country feel left out. The francophones outside Quebec, the
people who live north of the 60th parallel and the multicultural groups feel left out of this commission.
I want to ask a question of the Deputy Prime Minister or the Prime Minister-

-"suppleant". I will use the French term. This is not stalling.
He is the one who is stalled. [English]

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Will his government consider enlarging that commission to include the people I have just referred to and, second, will the report of that commission be given to Parliament eventually for analysis and action?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I know that the quality of my French sometimes leaves something to be desired in the country-
It is better than your English.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is better than my English, the former Primer Minister tells me. It is part of the rich diversity of Canada, and I am sure he would continue to encourage me to be inventive in my vocabulary if not in my response to questions.
The reason that we have established this commission is precisely because thousands, perhaps millions, of Canadians do in fact feel left out of decisions that affect the future of the country. I think that is a matter which has to be of concern to all of us who work within national institutions.
Our national institutions are obviously not working as well as they should. We have to continue to carry out our responsibilities in this place and in other national institutions, but we have to recognize the reality that Canadians feel left out, that they want an opportunity to participate in planning and deciding the future of this extraordinary country. We will all be the beneficiaries of that.
Are there likely to be changes in the composition of the panel that was established? No, there are not. Is there going to be a determined effort to ensure that every Canadian in every region from every background

has the opportunity to participate fully in this process? Yes, there is. That is why we put it in-

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
First of all, Madam Speaker, Mr. Remillard made a mistake yesterday because he referred to the $240 million forestry agreement when he should have mentioned the regional economic development agreement which has nothing to do with what we are talking about.
Second, with respect to the money spent by the federal government in Quebec and concerning the $800 million agreement, the federal government has earmarked about 76 per cent of the funds, and the Quebec government about 40 per cent. Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. This morning's release of the tanker safety report spells out
Oral Questions
an urgent agenda for the protection of Canada's four coasts from tanker spills and dumping.
This morning at the press conference, the minister's talked in vague terms of studying, examining and assessing. The report predicts we can expect one major spill every year and it says we are utterly unprepared now.
Will the minister take immediate steps to obtain the necessary funds and staff to implement as much of the report as possible without having to proceed to legislation?

Madam Speaker, I want to take this opportunity on behalf of the government, and I think all Canadians, to thank David Brander-Smith and his panel for the report. It is certainly wide-ranging and very hard hitting and the government takes into account its recommendations. They are excellent.
We have only had the report for a short time, but my hon. friend makes the point that we should move as quickly as possible. Yes, we are. I think there are some things we can do to co-ordinate our responses between various departments to increase our surveillance and inspection. We will undertake to do those immediately. Vis-a-vis things that have been in the works for some time, I am pleased to advise my hon. friend that a $5.3 million installation of vessel traffic services will be made in Placentia Bay. That will be announced this afternoon by my hon. friend, the Minister for International Trade.

Madam Speaker, the minister's response is a bit more positive than it was at the press conference this morning. I would encourage him to quickly prepare a plan and table it before Parliament.

Will the minister make good on his government's alleged commitment to consultation? Will this government move to overturn the agency's decision?

I was hoping my friend would return to Brander-Smith so I can improve my answers.

Oral Questions
No, I do not think that the decision will make any difference to the vigilance which the government will show toward all of the VIA routes in this country. The last VIA route cuts were as a result of a determination as to where we could best spend the taxpayers' money. I think the results speak for themselves and I should not be worried if I were the travelling public.

Given the declining state of our shipping and harbour industry across Canada and the outright condemnation of this plan by the St. Lawrence Economic Development Council, how can the minister force Canadian shippers to pay these onerous user fees, knowing full well that this will destroy the competitiveness of the marine industry along the St. Lawrence Seaway, particularly in the province of Quebec which will be the hardest hit?

Madam Speaker, the government makes no apologies for looking at how we can best serve the shipping public and the Canadian taxpayer in organizing the Department of Transport. To that end we have looked at cost recovery and my hon. friend makes it sound as though it is a fait accompli. He knows very well that it is a consultation process. It is going on in the marine mode, it is going on in the aviation mode. Furthermore, my hon. friend also knows that the deadline for input to me was extended from November 1, 1990 to February 1, 1991 just last week.

My supplementary is for the same minister. This government, through its ill-conceived policies, also makes no apologies for derailing our trains, grounding our planes and bringing our airlines to a halt, and now they are trying to sink the shipping industry.
Now that it is clear that these user fees will devastate the competitive edge of the marine industry, will he come to his senses and reject and revoke the implementation of these damaging user fees to the marine industry?

Madam Speaker, as of now there are no "these user fees". There is a consultation process with the industry under way. I will await the end of that consultation process before I make any decision. That is when the decision will be made, based on consultation, not the way the Liberal Party used to do it.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, it is about time we had some action from this government and the government of British Columbia on the forest agreements.

In terms of what the Auditor General said, I do not know what report my hon. friend read, but I could not find any text that would come anywhere close to what he is alleging.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. Recently the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council added its voice to the rising chorus of those concerned about this government's transportation policies. The viability of the port of Halifax is being threatened by the ports in New York and U.S. rail lines. By the way, the port of Halifax contributes over half a billion dollars to the Atlantic economy and is responsible for thousands of jobs.
Will the minister finally address this pending economic disaster, order Canadian National Railways to upgrade its track between Montreal and Toronto, and take steps immediately to ensure that Ontario and Quebec bound container traffic is not being spirited away to the U.S. eastern seaboard ports.

November 2, 1990
Oral Questions

I am fully aware, Madam Speaker, of the concerns of the east coast, especially the port of Halifax, vis-a-vis transportation. I have toured the port of Halifax by helicopter and I have met with the Harbour Port Commission. We discussed their concerns for the future.
We presently have under way an initiative which we think will be helpful vis-a-vis the co-ordination of the two modes, rail and port. I am sure that my hon. friend will be interested in what we are doing. We think we can make some progress down there.

Madam Speaker, the time for action by this minister is now. He has been made aware of the problem over the last six months on a number of occasions.
If he needs any further evidence that the threat is real, and the threat is today, I have in my possession a document which was presented before the Interstate Commerce Commission by Hapag-Lloyd, who just happens to be the fourth largest shipper into the port of Halifax. When will the minister start taking his job seriously and start protecting Canadian jobs, instead of transporting Canadian jobs in the marine industry to the ports in New York and New Jersey?

I want to advise the House, Madam Speaker, that I have been made aware of the concerns of the port of Halifax by colleagues on this side of the House. My hon. friend has never once raised them in this House.
I want to inform my hon. friend that CN is presently upgrading the line between Halifax and Montreal. Those things are already being acted upon.
That's right.

been discussing this issue for almost an hour and we discussed it for a full day very recently. This is no doubt an important question. However, I do not think that it would be appropriate to set aside the matters before the House today in order to have an emergency debate. Maybe some other time.

Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to be able to respond on behalf of my party to the motion placed before the House by the member for Haldimand-Norfolk.
It is a very timely motion to be debating in the House as we witness the unfolding of the GATT negotiations on the one hand, and the extremely tough times which Canadian farm families are facing on the other.
Farming has never been easy in this country. The vagaries of weather and markets, and the mechanization of the farm industry and its effect on the farm community have all contributed to a great deal of uncertainty over the years and never made farming an easy way of life. However, the current crisis bears more serious attention than it has been getting. Part of the problem is that as the farm population dwindles, it becomes less and less significant, politically. Therefore, the issues pertaining to agriculture have received much less attention than they should have because of the very significant role of agriculture, not only in our national economy but particularly because of rural Canada where one-third of Canadians still live.
This decline goes all the way back to 1981. That is why I would like to put a few figures before the House that we, as members, might look at as we contemplate what is happening to the farm community.
For example, in 1989 farmers received only 80 per cent of the income for livestock and grains that they produced that they received in 1981. In other words, from 1981 to 1989, the amount that they received in cash for their production was only 80 per cent of the original figure. At the same time, production costs went up 150 per cent. So you can see that the gap between what farmers receive for their products, through the marketplace, as compared to what they have to pay in expenses has opened up very, very significantly.
This year alone we are looking at a 37 per cent drop in net farm income and a 60 per cent cut in the province of Saskatchewan, the province from which I come and where my father still farms and where I still live, a proud mortgage payer on a half section of land which I have at this point rented out.
This is not merely a statistical problem. This is very much a human problem. Obviously, when you go that long with such a big gap between income and expenses, the debt load piles up, particularly with the high interest rate policies which first Liberal governments and then Conservative governments have consistently pursued, ensuring that farmers who got into the industry, in the sixties to the mid-seventies, have continually been paying very high charges on the money that they have borrowed.
This has not only created uncertainty in the farm community, but it has now come to the point where the debt the younger generation is taking on is even dragging down their parents. Parents offer collateral for loans that the younger generation has taken on, never dreaming that their retirement incomes would suddenly be wiped out as creditors come calling. This is happening repeatedly throughout rural Canada.
As well, there is an increase in stress for farm families as income earners need to go to other provinces to bring home income to keep the farms going. This creates all kinds of stress, not only on the farm families but it also robs the community of its base of people who can keep community activities going. Furthermore, we have a real sense of hopelessness. Young people do not want to farm

and are looking for the first opportunity to get off the farm if only they could get their money out. This is certainly not the kind of scenario where a vibrant, rural community can evolve.
Part of our problem is that we have always looked exclusively at agriculture and not looked at what is happening to the population. We have accepted this decline because we have not looked at the population and made the maintenance of a rural and farm population one of our goals and priorities as a society.
Part of the problem is that the real crisis with regard to the rural population has been masked somewhat by the phenomenon around urban centres where there has been a great deal of acreage development and a moving of people from the cities to the rural areas around cities. I certainly have no opposition to that. There are a lot of people who have done that around the city of Prince Albert. The community of Spruce Home, where I live, has a lot of people who have moved out from the city. Nevertheless, this inflates the rural numbers which show up in census figures while the actual fact is that the genuine rural community that is not influenced by an urban centre close by has been in deep trouble. For example, in Saskatchewan between 1981 and 1989 we have had a decrease of 1,000 farmers a year, down to 60,000, in spite of all the claims previous governments made to support the farming sector.
Currently, of those 60,000 farmers, 10,000 are living with the daily threat of foreclosure. They have received notice of foreclosure and are currently at some stage in the process of losing some or all of their farm assets. Those 10,000 farmers could well be gone in the very near future, given the cash flow situation on the prairies. It is a very cruel joke that there are wonderful crops of grain but there is no market for it and no money for it when it is sold.
This spills over into small-town Canada. If you look again at my home province of Saskatchewan, of the 701 communities there 303, almost half the communities in the province, the population has diminished since 1986. That represents failed businesses, closed schools, and a lack of services right across rural Saskatchewan. In many
Supply
ways, this same situation pertains to many other parts of the country.
When we look at the whole process of what has happened to agriculture, we can look back to the year 1969 and the task force report on agriculture. That report essentially said that two out of three farmers were inefficient and had to go. The report was roundly condemned by all sectors of the farm community. It was never fully adopted by any government. Certainly, the Liberal government of the day did not embrace it with open arms and the Conservative government since then has not embraced it.
However, in my mind the policies included in that, the acceptance of the notion that two out of three farmers were inefficient and had to go, has served as the underpinning of agricultural policy in this country. The trend outlined in that task force report has clearly been operative since that time.
The rural community has finally recognized what is happening and is saying: "We have retreated long enough. We fought enough rear-guard actions. We have to draw the line". There will be no more retreat by rural Canadians when it comes to their way of life, their population and their future.
The motion deals with a number of underpinnings which have made it possible to maintain what we have now by way of a rural community, as well as in the future. Certainly, orderly marketing and supply management have worked in most respects very well. That is why I find it very distressing that they are under attack.
They are under attack by editorialists in this country. It is an ill-informed and virulent attack, reminiscent in many ways of the attack by Mrs. Beryl Plumptre and others during the late 1970s who were supposedly fighting inflation and were using that as a platform to attack farm incomes. Many Canadians believe that marketing boards never recovered from the attacks launched on it.
At the same time we have the waffling of a government that says on one hand it fully supports supply management, but on the other hand introduced a free trade agreement which allows much greater access of American exports into the Canadian market. That goes along with an equivalent producer subsidy analysis of farm subsidies at GATT which end up greatly distorting the true picture of subsidies in Canadian agriculture,

Supply
because that formula includes the prices farmers get under supply-management as a subsidy. That is not correct at all. That is a price that is coming out of the marketplace and is not a subsidy. However, with the way we have allowed the GATT negotiations to proceed, that is considered a subsidy and something we are prepared to put on the table. When it comes to supply management and subsequent discussions, what we have to get away from, not only in this country but internationally is the whole beggar thy neighbor approach to world trade and agriculture where the multinational corporations are allowed to control the price of agriculture production around the world. They ratchet down the prices to farmers and ratchet up the input costs, leaving farmers poorer and competing with each other for a shrinking over-all farm dollar.
We do not want to make farmers in Europe, the United States or the Third World any poorer. I am worried that the so-called liberalization of trade that we see is essentially an abandonment of the world trade system to the multinational corporate sector and will do nothing but further depress farm incomes around the world.
Something that affects farmers in my part of the country very much is the whole question of the Crow benefit. The Crow rate was an historic agreement in this country. In my mind it was a part of the west's constitutional deal with Canada. It allowed us to move our product to export markets as part of a deal we had with the rest of Canada to make it viable to produce grain on the prairies. That was undermined by preceding Liberal governments which chipped away at it through the Western Grain Transportation Act.
The Crow benefit is under attack again. This is an attack that the farm community has almost unanimously resisted through their farm organizations. It is under attack through the transportation task force which very much distorted the whole grain transportation picture and its analysis. It came out with a very tilted kind of analysis in favour of a pay-the-producer type of regime. At the same time, our government bureaucrats and people making these decisions are continuing the undermining of the Crow benefit by using GATT as an excuse to get rid of the benefit to prairie farmers.
The point is that the U.S. or any of the other trading partners have never said that the Crow benefit is a problem to them. That is a problem we are imposing on ourselves.
The government argues that it has provided all kinds of money to agriculture over the last number of years and indeed it has. A lot of that money has been ad hoc. A lot of that money that has been given to the farming community shows that the government is essentially schizophrenic in its approach to agriculture. On the one hand there is a supposed commitment to supply management and orderly marketing. On the other hand, oats are removed from the Wheat Board and the free trade deal very soon will allow competition with the Wheat Board in our Canadian markets.
When it comes to grain, one sees the elimination of the fuel rebate, new costs to crop insurance and the flip-flop on grain cash advances which undermines orderly marketing. Then the government comes forward with task force reports. The farm community looks forward to these task force reports with some openness of mind and with some hope that a more coherent approach to agriculture will result.
To give credit to the government, the whole picture has not fully come into focus as yet. The Gross Revenue Income Plan, GRIP, reminds me very much of the plan that we proposed in the last federal election whereby grain producers would be assured the cost of production on their first $8,000 of production. That would be a guaranteed price on a guaranteed amount of production. It would give farmers certainty and it would be simple to administer. It was something the NDP proposed in the election and was very well received. The closer the GRIP program comes to that kind of concept, the better it will work.
The NISP, the Net Income Stabilization Plan, I fear is going to help only those farmers who already have a substantial net income. This would apply to the older farmers and leave the younger farmers in the situation where they are virtually as high and dry as they are now. If we look at what is happening in my own province of Saskatchewan, the average family income of the Saskatchewan farmer from agriculture this year will be $5,000. There is no family in Canada that can live on $5,000. Some immediate help is needed and also some long-term income insurance.
While I am speaking of the net farm income picture with regard to farm families, however, I would like to make note of another issue that is not often addressed in this House. That is the situation confronting the combined income farmers in this country. At least 50 per

cent of the farmers by now rely to some degree or other on off-farm income to maintain their family income. This is hardly surprising when the income from farming averages $5,000.
What happens to these farmers is that they are subject to the Income Tkx Act which does nothing but creates uncertainty for them through something called section 31 of the Income Thx Act. This section makes very uncertain whether farmers who have off-farm income can write off their farm losses against that income, something that every other business in this country can do. Farmers, however, are subject to section 31 of the Income Tax Act which allows Revenue Canada to determine whether that is a bona fide loss or not. It can adjust a farmer's taxation in accordance with its rulings which are very vague, which are very general, and which are very hard to apply in advance. In fact, Revenue Canada is able to go after a farmer for as long as four years after the last tax filing and reassess that farmer's income.
While farmers are putting their own money into their own income insurance plans and their own investment into their farms, they are doing so with the threat that the tax man can come along and lop off their heads in one fell swoop with application of section 31 of the Income Tkx Act. I plead with this government to look at that act. As the farm income situation has worsened more and more farmers are vulnerable to that kind of situation, and it needs to be dealt with.
In the last minutes that I have left I would like to indicate briefly some of the policies that our party would like to advocate to ensure that there are no more retreats for rural Canada, that we do not have to turn around and fight any more rear guard actions.
First, we need to plough ahead with the whole safety net concept. We have to make sure that we recognize that this industry cannot be solely market driven, that there needs to be intervention by the public sector, that we need to work together co-operatively, and that the orderly marketing system is what is going to keep us afloat in the future.
These programs will not be in effect until next year, as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture said. This year in Saskatchewan alone we need $1.1
Supply
billion to maintain the farmers there at their current very poor net income level. We need an immediate injection of cash into the farm community.
We need lower interest rates in the farm community. No sector has suffered more from high interest rates than the farm sector. We need reform of the Farm Credit Corporation so that it is not just acting like another lender out there in the marketplace and that in fact it uses its potential role to set up new farmers, to keep farmers in business, to provide long-term leasing provisions and to provide low interest rates so that farmers are not continually caught, generation after generation, paying interest on the farm debt, buying the farm from each other, and keeping each other at a low income level and in uncertainty generation after generation.
We need to make sure that our rural infrastructure does not deteriorate any further. We have to stop the closure of post offices which undermines rural communities. We have to make sure that rural services by VIA Rail and the rural highway system are maintained. We have to make sure that the co-operative sector is not sunk by the GST being applied to investments and to co-operative dividends so that rural communities and farmers can keep organizing co-operatives, as they have so successfully in the past to help themselves.
In conclusion, I am very happy that we have been able to address question. In this country people still want to farm. We have the land to farm on. The world still needs our food. All we lack is the vision or the political will to make sure that we maintain a vibrant farm community in the future.

Madam Speaker, I salute the member for Prince Albert-Churchill River. When the member talked about a vision toward the end of his speech, I thought immediately of a saying of John F. Kennedy. When he decided to take on the space project in 1961 he said: "We are going to put a man on the moon". Nobody really knew the various technical ramifications and complexities involved in putting a man on the moon. But, because he had a vision, he was able to rally the people of the United States of America. People from all walks of life, professionals and school kids worked toward that common cause.

Supply
When I listened to the member today I heard about the various things we in this country have been doing for agriculture. He talked about the various aspects of life affected by agriculture. It seems that we have to develop a whole new equation, not unlike the equation that John F. Kennedy developed when he put a man on the moon.
Traditionally we have been a country where our thought process has been measuring strength by bankers we know and armaments we build, but maybe we should be shifting our thought process to becoming a nation that measures its strength by the mouths we feed and the environment we protect. When we get into a thought process where we measure our nation's strength by how many people we feed and how much environment we protect, we are talking about a totally new language.
The member was bom, raised, and is now involved in this field. My question to him is: Is it not time that we should develop totally new approaches to measuring the strength of agriculture in our country, its role in our country and its relationships with other countries around the world and to measuring true strength in terms of a country?

Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood very much for his very thoughtful question.
He captured in some ways where I believe we need to be heading. As I tried to outline in my speech, part of our problem has been that we lack that kind of a vision. We had it when we originally settled this country. John A. Macdonald's national policy was one of filling up the countryside. Nowadays we would apply an EARP process to the whole matter of cutting down trees, developing roads, and so on. Nevertheless, at that time we had a broad vision of the development of this country which really excited the imagination not only of the country but of the whole world as immigrants poured into this country. We developed rail networks and other infrastructure around the development of the rural community in its capacity to produce food not only for Canada but for the world.
Gradually we have lost that. It is hard to say whether it was the chicken or egg first in this case, whether we lost the vision and thus became vulnerable to death by a thousand wounds of the farm or rural community as one program and another were developed which undermined
not only the economics and the population base but the broader vision of the rural community.
It is a very sound approach to analysing the future. I am glad in the sense that the government has included sustainability as part of the four pillars to which it wants to address itself. I have some skepticism about that, given the fact that the government's over-all approach is clearly one of having a more market driven economy and of letting the chips fall where they may, a kind of approach which many of us feel in no way will lead us toward a more sustainable future.
Nevertheless, it is on the table and part of that certainly has to be a new sense that we are protecting a large environment as well. We are not only producers of food. We are custodians of a vast percentage of the earth's land service. We have a trust. It is to look after this land not only for our own future populations but for the world at large so that it stays productive in future generations.
We can encompass that kind of vision. We can come to terms with what that really means and set some firm, concrete objective for ourselves in terms of no more rural depopulation, maintenance of rural services, or what we want to do as a society. I think we can make great progress.
Two very specific things need to be done right now to start that process along. First, I am very concerned that the task forces, as good as they are, have no unifying theme. No analysis is to be done or is available or nothing else is envisioned that will tie all those task forces together into a comprehensive view of where all this takes us. It is still going to be a fragmented approach as each task force reports in each sector.
We will not know whether we stay in retreat or whether in fact we move forward on a comprehensive basis, at least not on the basis of what is being done through the task forces.
The global view has to be included as part of the process, and that is not part of it. We need to tie together our thinking on rural development as well. There are a lot of very creative thinkers around this country, both in the academic community and in farm organizations such as the wheat pools, the Farmers' Union and a vast number of other farm organizations. Also there are some very creative thinkers at the community level.

People do not want to see these communities decline. They have good ideas.
We need to develop a mechanism to tie together rural development thinking and take it forward on a sustained basis, in a manner that we as parliamentarians can have input and show some national leadership to achieve what the member so eloquently suggested, a new vision whereby we measure ourselves by the mouths we feed and the environment we protect.

Madam Speaker, I just want to comment briefly on the hon. member's speech.
I was struck by the frankness and especially the depth of the hon. member's speech. I can say that as the member for Chambly, a riding next door to that of Madam Speaker, and in fact after actually living in Madam Speaker's riding, in the small town of Saint-Bar-nabe-Sud, I have known for a long time that farmers are extremely worried about- The Tories on the other side seem to think this is funny. I don't think it is funny at all.
The people in my riding and the town where I live, the farmers, are very worried. You can smile all you want. You can smile while you are the government, but you won't be there much longer!
What I was saying, Madam Speaker, is that the farmers are worried for two reasons: first, they see a government that poses a daily threat, with programs like the GST, with interest rates so high they can't even survive, and free trade, Madam Speaker. Madam Speaker, this is sickening.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is my pleasure today to participate in this debate on the motion proposed by my colleague, the hon. member for Haldimand-Norfolk.
We are talking today about the worry that Canadian farmers have concerning these negotiations on the GATT. Canadian farmers want us to be speaking in the House of Commons on the policies of this government with regard to agriculture. And, of course, as I said previously, they are extremely concerned.

Canadian dairy farmers, and especially those in Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, as I said earlier, feel threatened. There are about 1,000 dairy farmers in my riding. I see the Secretary of State for External Affairs across the way, and I know he is very familiar with the electoral district of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. I have good reason to believe he visits my riding at least once a week, in fact just a few kilometres from my home.
He is familiar with farming in Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. He has a chance to see farming firsthand, since it is the main industry in my riding.
Madam Speaker, Canadian farmers are worried about the message being sent by the government opposite. On October 15 in the House of Commons, the Minister for International Trade said, and I quote verbatim from Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, on October 1, we had to file at Geneva, together
with other countries involved in this negotiation, an estimate of the
costs of various programs in effect in Canada to assist agriculture.
The total was $8.8 billion. The Minister of Agriculture should be
ashamed at the amount of assistance he is giving Canadian farmers.
It is a huge amount of assistance.
Madam Speaker, the Minister for International Trade may have said this jokingly, but I can assure you his comments are disturbing. I hope no one in this country shares the minister's view that we have $8.8 billion worth of farm subsidies, that we should be ashamed of the amount of assistance being given to Canadian farmers and that it is a huge amount. That is not true.
First of all, if we talk about Canadian dairy farmers and the net worth of the supply management systems in this country, the fact that the price paid to farmers or, if you prefer, the fact that farmers have a guaranteed income for their products, that is, a guaranteed income per unit, the more efficient they are, the bigger their

Supply
profits. So what is guaranteed is not the farmer's profits but the price he gets for his milk, and that is calculated according to a formula based on production costs.
Some people have put a value of $2.2 billion on this. However, Madam Speaker, this is merely an assumption, because the federal government's grants to dairy farmers total $266 millions, which is only 10 per cent of that amount. There are those who would see this as a subsidy. I say it is a non-existent subsidy.
I have in front of me an article which appeared recently in The Ottawa Citizen. It is about a farmer by the name Nathan Harris from Renfrew county. Mr. Harris was complaining to The Ottawa Citizen about a story that had been written concerning subsidies to agriculture. He had been complaining with reason. I will read the article:
Specifically, he was worried-not to say fuming just a bit-about an Oct. 17 column by Citizen columnist John Hay on the subject of farm subsidies.
"This sort of report," said Harris, "is totally unacceptable."
What particularly irked him was Hay's statement that Canadian dairy farmers "cream off" $2.2 billion a year in government subsidies. (Harris also wasn't very happy at Hay's description of Canada's dairy supply management program: "price-fixing and supply-rigging by marketing boards.")
That subsidy figure was wildly inflated, said Harris. After all, there are about 36,000 dairy farmers in Canada and $2.2 billion would average out to something like $60,000 per farmer-
Obviously, Mr. Harris is quite correct in pointing out that dairy farmers do not get anything like that from the federal government. The article states further:
Still, when I asked columnist Hay the source of his figures, his answer was immediate: "The government of Canada." The federal trade department-
That is the same department that is led by the Minister for International Trade who is telling us that the Minister of Agriculture should be ashamed of giving, according to him, so much help to the farming community. Jane Huntley of Dairy Farmers of Canada explained the facts. She stated:
The $2.2. billion-is not a government payment to dairy fanners.
In fact, about 85 per cent of it-$ 1.87 billion-is accounted for by the
difference between the Canadian domestic price and the prevailing
world price for dairy products.
This so-called prevailing world price for dairy products includes producer subsidies that other countries give to their producers. This has an effect of lowering the price artificially in those countries. The difference between our price and the artificially lowered price is deemed to be a subsidy.
It does not take an economic genius to know that that does not make sense. If their prices are artificially deflated, then surely we should not take the difference between them and our price in order to arrive at what is the so-called rightful price.
In any case, what difference does it make when our supply management system is designed to sustain our Canadian consumers and not for export. In other words, supply management is not a trade distortion measure. Because it is not, the whole point of what the Minister for International Tbade said in reply to that question on October 15, 1990 in the House of Commons is wrong.
Those from other countries who are telling us that our dairy farmers are getting these kinds of subsidies are wrong. As I said previously, the dairy farmers of Canada get only about 10 to 15 per cent of the amount that some have claimed our farmers are getting.

Madam Speaker, let us not misread public opinion in this country. I have here a document prepared by the Dairy Farmers of Canada concerning a poll carried out earlier this year by Goldfarb Consultants.
The findings by Goldfarb Consultants were as follows: 85 per cent of the people who responded to this poll described the job done by Canadian dairy farmers as either good or excellent; 77 per cent felt that Canadian dairy farmers did a job as good or better than their counterparts in other countries; 79 per cent felt that the lives of dairy farmers are very hard; and 94 per cent that dairy producers scrupulously meet the standards of the industry.
If I were a Tory member, Madam Speaker, I would envy these findings.

I can assure you that the level of trust which Canadian consumers have in our agricultural industry is far greater than their level of trust in the government opposite.
Madam Speaker, some may feel that it is not important for our industry to be self-reliant. Again, you know, the same poll revealed other interesting facts. To wit: 94 per cent of Canadians feel that it is important for the Canadian dairy industry to be self-reliant. The following question brought to light some interesting facts: What importance should the dairy industry have in Canada? One choice was: important enough to meet our own needs with surpluses to export. Seventy-five per cent of Canadians agreed with this statement. Madam Speaker, this demonstrates the Canadians' trust in the system.
To conclude, Madam Speaker, I should like to quote a statement which the Minister of Finance made on October 15 in this House, as reported on page 14138 in Hansard: "But you cannot go to heaven without dying." Madam Speaker, I can tell you that my colleagues and I will not allow Canadian farmers to die a slow death.

Madam Speaker, I too am very pleased to be speaking in the House today in support my colleague's motion "that in the upcoming GATT negotiations and in over-all economic policies, the government recognize the essential role played by farmers in maintaining the Canadian way of life".
I believe it is essential that the government be given a strong message. The message is that Canada's farmers deserve our loyalty and our support, that the principles on which these people built their livelihoods must be maintained.
The GATT negotiations are on the minds of all Canadian farmers today. Agricultural subsidies are seen by many observers to be at the centre of the current round of GATT negotiations. Many questions still remain as to the possible outcome of these talks.
These questions, as we all know, have an enormous impact on our agricultural sector in Canada. There could be major repercussions for the farmers in my community of Nepean as an example.
Supply
Let me briefly outline the Canadian government's proposal that it took to the GATT negotiation table. The position is as follows. First, 100 per cent elimination of all existing export subsidies over a ten-year period; second, all non-tariff barriers, other than supply management will be converted to their tariff equivalents; third, new tariff equivalents will be reduced by 50 per cent over a ten-year period and at the end of the ten-year period no tariff will be greater than 20 per cent; fourth, eliminate meat import laws and replace them with the safeguard measures provided in Article XIX of the GATT, fifth, reduce by 50 per cent all trade distorting internal support programs over a ten-year period; sixth, double all allowable amounts of supply managed imports entering Canada to 5 per cent, subject to U.S. and EEC participation.
Madam Speaker, let me speak specifically to the issue of supply management. Let me preface it by saying that this position represents the minimum requirement for Canadian fanners.
The Canadian government has made the fundamental mistake, right from the outset, of offering 5 per cent on imports as their opening bid. According to the dairy industry, this is the bottom line position. I had occasion to sit at a meeting with half a dozen of the dairy farmers from my particular area of Ottawa-Carleton and they are very concerned about this. We will have to wait and see what will result from this blunder. I am standing here in the House today in order to encourage the government to hold to this bare minimum. There is no room for movement on this issue.
Canada's challenge at this point is to develop an economically viable agricultural industry that can compete successfully in a competitive and liberalized international trading environment. Canadian negotiators must keep this most basic goal in mind throughout the ongoing negotiating process.
Within this framework, Canada must work within the GATT, first, to create a fair and clear set of international trading rules for agriculture and, second, build a system where access to markets around the world would be increased through the reduction of world tariff and non-tariff barriers.

November 2, 1990
Supply
We, in the Liberal Party, feel it is through international trading arrangements that liberalization should occur, with less of a direct focus on the bilateral relationship with the United States. This is why the current Uruguay round of negotiations is so important. So far, the federal government has proven itself unable to get the backing for its Article XI proposal; far too willing to slash internal programs, including dairy programs by 50 per cent; and too agreeable in undermining supply management in Canada by negotiating the elimination of tariffs of all agricultural goods in the FTA.
It is essential for Canada to maintain its long held principles of supply management. In a country of this size, with pressures from all round, it is necessary to ensure the existence of safety nets. These safety nets are an essential part of the agricultural industry in Canada. Without them, the industry would be in quite dire circumstances. In order that a stable and secure agriculture industry be maintained in Canada, management must be sustained.
I also want to point out that it has not gone unnoticed that the federal government appears to be trying to play farm interests in the east against those in the west, in hopes of recovering western support. This is a very dangerous game. The federal government is not going to gain the support of one community at the expense of another community. This would fracture the Canadian farming community, and I consider this to be unacceptable and unprincipled. It is time for the federal government to adopt the role of a national, not regional, advocate.
The Canadian farmer deserves our support and a fair return on his investment of labour and love for farming. We should be refocusing our attention back towards self-sufficiency in food. This motion is an important symbol of our support for the Canadian farmers' efforts to feed Canadians in the years to come.
Canada has relied on its farmers in the past, and I believe that we will need to rely on them more in the future. It is up to us, here in this place, to show that we are on their side and that we want them to succeed.
In closing, I want to say that agriculture is an integral cog in the Canadian economy. Even more important, the Canadian farmer is of fundamental importance to the
Canadian way of life and the well being of the Canadian nation.
It has been a real honour and a privilege to speak on this agricultural issue in the House today and to indicate my support to the farming industry here in Canada.

Madam Speaker, earlier today I paid very close attention to the speeches of my two opposition colleagues, the one made by the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell and what was intended to be a speech by the member for Chambly. Mr. Speaker, what little hair I have on the head stood straight up.
I was very surprised to hear the hon. member for Chambly speak on agriculture in the House. I suspect he may never have seen a cow in his life and, in light of his remarks about farmers being against the GST, I would guess he knows precious little about the subject. Mr. Speaker, if anybody stands to benefit from the implementation of the GST, it has to be the farming community, and so far they have been enthusiastic about it.
As to my colleague the hon. member for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell, for whom I have a lot of respect and esteem, he at least-unlike the member for Chambly who just had the floor-knows what he is talking about because his riding is home to a good many agricultural producers. But that is as far as I can go in terms of congratulations to the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. A moment ago he began preaching as he is wont to do, trying to tell us how considerate the Liberals are with farmers, how they see things, and how they have now discovered the pressing needs of the agricultural community in Quebec and in Canada.
Strange that we should hear that from the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. I can still remember back in 1983 when Jean Chretien was the member for Saint-Maurice. Fed up because local farmers had demonstrated in front of his Shawinigan riding office he said to the newspapermen: "Farmers are a bunch of cry babies, and there is nothing we can do for them. The more they get, the more they want". That was Jean Chretien's position in 1983-84. All of a sudden, Mr. Speaker, we find out that the Liberals are fascinated by agricultural issues.
November 2, 1990

I would suggest that the member for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell review his speech, and while he is at it he should give a few pointers on agriculture to the member for Chambly who is in the House and who earlier made the worst speech on agriculture that I have heard so far in this session. I urge him to get together with his colleague in the agricultural caucus and ask for a few hints. Then he could come back to see me because back home we are familiar with the problems experienced by the farming community. In Saint-Maurice I have producers from practically all the farm specialties you are likely to see in Quebec.
The member for Chambly was making comparisons and concluded that agriculture is on the brink of disaster. He was referring to the riding of our Deputy Speaker, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe, which happens to be next to his. Now and then he would be well advised to look around when he goes to Saint-Hyacinthe.
Mr. Speaker, for the benefit of people who are unaware of this fact I can tell you that Saint-Hyacinthe agricultural producers are the richest and most highly rated. They are Quebec's producers who live in total prosperity and, in terms of agriculture, the riding stands second to none. That is a fact. We know these people have managed to rationalize their operations over the years, with the result that the Saint-Hyacinthe region has become extremely prosperous indeed. This should be obvious to anyone who visits the town of Saint-Hyacinthe the surrounding area, Mr. Speaker.
Next time, I suggest that before the hon. member for Chambly, rises in the House to speak to a subject he is totally unfamiliar with, he should at least do his homework. I realize members cannot be expected to know everything, Mr. Speaker. However, when a member takes the trouble to rise in the House to speak in debate as the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell did earlier, although I do not agree with the hon. member, at least he knows about farming. And I wish the hon. member for Chambly would get this straight. A member does not take the floor just to provide window dressing, because he happens to be the only member from Quebec in his caucus. A member rises in the House when he has something worthwhile to say.
Supply
Mr. Speaker, today, I would like the House to consider for a moment the position being defended by Canadian negotiators in the last stretch of the Uruguay Round which is drawing to a close after four years of intense discussions by 98 GATT member states.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, although agriculture represents only of 15 negotiating groups in this GATT round, it has become the focus of attention because of its efforts to get out of the present impasse. The problem is due mainly to the failure of major farm product exporting and importing countries to establish some order in a market that is characterized by anarchy. The situation is also due to a lack of clearcut rules applying to all partners in the agricultural sector.
In accordance with the instructions issued by the president of the negotiating group on agriculture, on October 15 our country tabled its detailed proposal for use in the multilateral talks on agricultural trade. I may recall that this is merely an initial proposal, conditional on the commitment of other trading partners to clean up their agricultural trading practices.
Canada's proposal consists of four main components, to be implemented over a period of ten years. Mr. Speaker, I noticed the hon. member for Chambly was listening carefully to what I was saying. I may add, for his benefit, that what is important for Quebec farmers is that negotiations are taking place, and Canada is not the only country involved. Ninety-eight other countries are involved in the talks. So why the defeatist attitude? Why these cries of gloom and doom about the future of agriculture in Quebec and Canada?
When he came to Saint-Tite, in the Champlain riding, he said that as far as farming was concerned, within six months of the implementation of the Free Hade Agreement, Saint-Tite would become a ghost town. Well, today, in Saint-Tite and everywhere else in the Quebec heart land, farmers are living well; granted, they may be worried, but they trust us and know for sure that the government of Canada will stand steadfast in supporting them.
Having briefly described where I stand on this issue, Mr. Speaker, I thank you.
