Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Canadian public in general must have been enlightened when they heard my friend the hon. member for Saint-Maurice. The way he took me to task is quite revealing about himself and his government. I must say that I understand, for I realize that my hon. colleague is very busy, having a great many things to do. He is very fond of his colleagues, and that is the reason why he spoke constantly while I was on my feet.
We indulge in psychology!

I am not sure he heard me. I am not sure either of his open mindedness. When dealing with the farm industry, I would say he demonstrated a certain narrow mindedness, if not out-right arrogance. Let me show you. He said: "The hon. member for Chambly is talking through his hat, but as representative of the Saint-Maurice riding, I do, and things are just fine". Frankly, Mr. Speaker, things are going badly! If I could only catch my hon. colleague's attention for one minute, I should like him to answer a question: Would you deny, in the House today, that the Minister of Agriculture has already predicted a 25 per cent loss of revenues in the farm industry? Hventy-five per cent! This information does not come from an Edmonston's report but a government's report. Find out for yourself! That is a fact. Of course there are farms in Saint-Hyacinthe which are doing well. But there are others, in Chambly and elsewhere, where the situation is bad, as the people will tell the hon. member for Saint-Maurice. Mr. Speaker, Jacques Proulx, of the UPA, will tell him that the situation is bad. Mr. and Mrs. Lareau are working a farm in my riding with their two sons, David and Martin.
This may seems strange to my hon. friend who will certainly refuse to believe me, but I spent a whole day working on Mr. and Mrs. Lareau's farm to find out what it meant to work on a dairy farm. Mr. Speaker, I had never worked on a farm. I am a newspaperman, a city boy. It is true. I am not trying to hide it.
Milk comes from cows!

That is right. But once elected, I decided that if ever I had to talk about the farm industry and other related problems, I should have a certain knowledge of the subject. Today, however, I don't think that the farmers both in Saint-Hyacinthe and Chambly
deserved my colleague's remarks which were full of arrogance and showed a complete lack of information.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The hon. member for Saint-Maurice. A short reply please.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, even though I would have liked to give a more complete answer.
First of all, he accused me of attacking him. The hon. member for Chambly was the first one to rise in this House to unfairly attack government policies without valid arguments by talking about the GST, which will in fact benefit the agricultural sector in general, as the Quebec farmers union publicly recognizes. It is the kind of thing the hon. member for Chambly said to us.
Since he is a lemon expert, he should stick to his specialty and only take part in debates on the subject of defective cars. But, if he does not know anything about agricultural issues, he should leave the floor to the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, to my colleague, the hon. member for Drummond, or to other knowledgeable members of this House instead of talking nonsense as he is doing today. It is quite regrettable, and he is misleading Quebec farmers.

Mr. Speaker, I would first like to state that it is admirable that my hon. colleague from the New Democratic Party would even enter the debate on agriculture. He recognizes that agriculture and agricultural issues are important to all Canadians. I welcome his intervention, but it is too bad that sometimes we have to get on a personality debate. I do not think that really adds to what we are trying to achieve here.
With respect to safety nets in the agricultural sector, I think the real safety net that Canadian farmers have today are the ministers responsible for agriculture, and the Minister for International Hade and the Prime Minister who made agriculture the subject of the GATT debate today under the Uruguay round. That is a safety net that no one opposite mentioned. In fact, it was the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Grains and Oilseeds who came up with some very imaginative programs to assist Canadian farmers under terms that they would not be addressed under the present safety net systems or Western Grain Stabilization.
November 2, 1990

We have to remind Canadians that it was running deep in the hole financially and we as a government bailed it out. That was money that-
The farmers bailed it out.

And the government of Canada through the taxpayers of Canada bailed out the Western Grain Stabilization program. It was not an insignificant amount; hundreds of millions of dollars went into this.
Let us look at some of the other programs to deal with difficult times. It was the safety net thinking of the Minister of Agriculture that led him, with the approval of the Prime Minister, to spend $2.1 billion on special grains programs. That program alone probably saved more western farmers than almost any other program since World War II. That was a very, very significant program, paid for by the taxpayers of Canada. We admit it was ad hoc. Ad hoc programs are not the ones easily dealt with. It takes a tremendous amount of cash from the treasury. Clearly, we cannot forget that the safety net this country has does lie in the hands of a few men in control of our Department of Agriculture.
There can be criticism. I was in the House in the previous Parliament when, after announcing the few hundreds of millions of dollars in this program, the people in the opposition shouted that we should spend more. They were not even thinking that it does come from the taxpayers.
Earlier I heard the member from Saskatchewan saying that we need lots of low credit and lots of programs. Everything is "government will save the day for all the farmers". That is the sound of the old farmer's union group. There were a lot of people who knew how to become efficient farmers without first crying to the government.
A lot of them were farmer's union members.

Farmers do not like to cry to the government. They like to make their own money and they like to be able to be in the free market system. This government is trying everything to get them back to the
Supply
free market system and fair trade, to bring some sense to agricultural trade under GATT.
We have had to put some subsidization out. Let us not forget that the provinces were there, too, subsidizing, countering each other within this country. They are not innocent in putting money out to farmers. Maybe they have to, but we do not within our own country have a level playing field with regard to agricultural subsidies. I think that has to be addressed. I believe the first ministers of this country should get together from time to time and try to put in an equal program, not one that encourages artificial production at times, but something that gives us a level playing field.
When it comes to the politics of agriculture and what we should do in the future, we all know there is a new, you might say, right-wing party in western Canada called the Reform Party. It wants to make great inroads. Just south of my constituency, the leader, Mr. Preston Manning, asks the public to help him form an agricultural policy. It was reported on October 27 that at two meetings he is reported as having "stressed the importance of reducing government spending".
This is quite unique because some of the farming community would like to support this new initiative of the Reform Party, but if it looked at it very closely, it is actually the total opposite of what the New Democrats want to do, which would probably be to double expenditures in agriculture. We have the Reform Party which is going to start cutting what we have.
Look at some of the programs which we did put into place, such as the agri-food programs to assist agricultural production and innovation or the drought assistance program. We had a terrible drought. The hon. member from Saskatchewan knows how severe the drought was. The Government of Canada came in with $500 million or $850 million and then another $500 million this spring to assist those in those particular areas. The Reform Party would have reduced that amount and, I suppose, members sitting in the seats opposite would have doubled that amount and just run the deficit wild.
We'll speak for ourselves. You tell us your policy.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman will have a time to get up and reflect on the agricultural

Supply
policy and I am sure he would want to do so. But these are some of the facts that we have to look at.
We have a tremendous crop this year and low world prices. But where is the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds? I tell you, he is out selling the crop for us. I mean, he has done so much to sell the grain of this country. In fact, yesterday-
Caused by the free market.

Well, there you have it, the New Democrats are going to be the next salesmen of our grain, in some market that is artificial as can be. They are going to find people to double the price of grain when it is at maybe $150 a tonne; they will find markets for it at $300 a tonne. That is the kind of logic we get from across the way. A free market is just that. It is there and you have to be competitive in it. Obviously, the subsidies of the Europeans do not exactly help us in this particular case.
The minister, knowing full well the difficulties, has been out there and yesterday made the suggestion that it looks like we are going to have a very good grain movement right into the new year. The hon. member should know the board has taken up all its options. I guess they cannot reveal the exact nature of the sale but I want to tell you, the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds, by the way, has a farm of his own and if anybody can understand the plight of the farmer, it is our Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds. He has his fingers right down in the soil. He knows about the potatoes grown and the grain grown and the problems faced, because he has faced them himself.
Earlier on we heard an allegation that the goods and services tax is going to cost the farmers a lot of money. Here is something that ought to be considered. In fact, the Minister of Finance very clearly said, and this has been accepted by farmers, that the farmers would reduce their costs of production by $250 million with the goods and services tax. I can assure you that his predictions have been almost always right on while he has been the finance minister of this House of Commons for the last six years, not like the projections from across the way; not the absolutely ridiculous statements that came from across the way. He has been right on. Farmers will
welcome this tax to reduce their input costs, as they should.
Certainly they will deny that this is likely going to happen, but the facts bear it out. Go to your farm dealers and find out what is going to happen to machine costs. They are going to go down. Input costs for fertilizers and chemicals will all go down, but I do not hear anybody speaking about that.
How about the Minister of Agriculture?

Mr. Speaker, I see you motioning that my time is up. In closing, let me say that farmers do face some difficult times, but it is this administration which in the past was able to make and assess programs to the benefit of farmers, and they know it.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with some interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Portage-Interlake, the place where they closed the base. The officials from that town are writing all the members of Parliament to help the member's town get some business going. They must wonder what their own member has done on their own behalf if they are having to recruit all 295 of us to intervene.
We'll take all the help we can get.

This is about as contradictory as the member's remarks were. I think he got carried away in a flight of rhetoric and accused the members opposite of advocating a position where the government is going to run everything, pay everything and where there is going to be an unlimited amount of taxpayers' money sloshing through the farm sector and somehow or other tied in with some ancient sins of the National Farmers Union.
If the hon. member wants to attack the National Farmers Union and the wheat pools of this country and the orderly marketing system that those organizations have advocated through the years, he should come out and do so directly.
What this debate is all about today is whether or not we are going to maintain an orderly marketing system based on the Wheat Board, the marketing boards and those kinds of institutions which make sure that we do not have to come in constantly with government money, that the market works for the farmer, not against the farmer, that the farmer is not the total victim of weather and international situations, and so on.

It used to be that governments in this country were good at working the international market to Canada's benefit, something we seem to have lost over the last 10 years.
At the same time the member pledges firm allegiance to the free market system, saying that this is going to solve all our problems, he turns around and brags about the billions of dollars increasing adherence to the free market system has cost us. Certainly it is not only our adherence to the free market system, it is the free market system that the United States of America is supposedly engaging in. The greatest free marketer in the world was supposed to be Ronald Reagan. He was supposed to have introduced the idea.
Right. Right. It ain't working.

But where did export subsidies come from? Who has increased their export subsidies 40 per cent in the last year, starting to subsidize into their own market, and even into Canada? This is the model that the hon. member is suggesting for Canadian agriculture. At the same time, he is attacking the traditional pillars of Canadian agriculture, the orderly marketing system which has made it unique and has allowed more Canadian farmers to survive.
I would like to ask the hon. member on which side of the fence he is actually on. Is he advocating that the orderly marketing system give away to the free market system, or is he not?

Mr. Speaker, I am glad the hon. member brought me back to orderly marketing. Before I enter that discussion, let me assure him that I come from a farm where we sell pigs without a marketing board, but we have a dairy for which we have a marketing board, and those things are pretty much to stay intact, as they are.
He would advocate that we would even have a marketing board for hogs, but I do not think that is going to fly. But let me get back to something that is very fundamental. When I indicated to this Chamber that in fact we have brought in programs to spend money to assist with the needs of agriculture at certain times, like a safety net program, it was his party that voted against the supply bill that put all the money in the hands of farmers. Have him explain that to his farmers back home. When we brought in the supply bill to put money into western grain stabilization and to put money into the Canadian
Supply
Wheat Board overrun, it was his government that voted against it. Explain that to the people of Canada. If you support the farming and the agricultural policies of your own government, why do you vote against them? It makes no sense. Talking about being on both sides of the fence. Why wouldn't he and his party have supported those very things which he demands this government to do?
Because the government spending plans are a bunch of garbage.

There you go, Mr. Speaker. There you have the answer; just a little more rhetoric.
I am not on both sides of the fence. We have supported orderly marketing. We have done that. It has been stated again and again by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of Agriculture that in fact orderly marketing is one of our criteria. We have the right to have it within our own country.
We are debating the GATT. Naturally we think we are totally and unfairly treated by our trading partners. We are demanding that some orderly marketing be brought there because it assists all Canadian farmers, especially the ones that he represents.

Mr. Speaker, before I had the privilege of sitting in this House, I was, as you may recall, a member of the National Assembly, and at the time I represented a rural riding.
Back in the early 70s, I quickly became acquainted with the problems and concerns of farmers. At the time, there had been a major development in the agricultural sector, in Quebec and across Canada, and I am referring to the introduction of milk quotas, which turned out to be a very important and very profitable decision for our dairy farmers.
Recently, five representatives of the Union des produc-teurs agricoles du Quebec came to see me in my office. In the past, when they met at various locations in the riding I represent, in the Petite Nation valley or in Thurso, for instance, I often attended their meetings. That is when I gradually came to understand-and when I say understand, I should say I merely scratched the surface-the real problems of farmers.

November 2, 1990
Supply
Lately, our farmers have become increasingly concerned, because of the GATT talks and especially because of free trade. The decision on imports of yogurt and dairy products including ice cream from the United States brought things to a head, when Quebec saw its milk quotas drop by 5 per cent, in other words, producers of industrial milk in Quebec will have to cut production by 5 per cent.
So obviously they are concerned. But they are also concerned for a number of other reasons. When we look at the motion, we see the words: "safety nets". As others said earlier, the safety net is there to ensure stable incomes that cover our farmers' production costs. However, I feel that this particular safety net has mainly benefited the general public, because for years our farm producers have been very efficient in their operations.
If we look at the past 20 years, and these are the facts, these are not figures out of a hat, if we look at the facts, the agri-food sector has been extremely efficient, with the cheapest products on the market, compared with the textile industry, auto manufacturers, and so forth. Farm producers have been very efficient since costs have not increased that much, compared with all other products on the market. So we can't say that they have failed to keep their operations up to date. In fact, they have been extremely efficient.
Will present benefits, such as the quota system for commercial milk producers or the stabalization program, be at stake in the negociations? Will the assistance we provide our farmers have to be cut?
I have always said, Madam Speaker, that agriculture has become as important as national defence in this world. If were to depend on outside sources for our food supplies, we would be putting ourselves in an extremely precarious situation. It is therefore essential-it is one of the most fundamental policies of our country-to ensure our self-sufficiency. There is no other choice. Otherwise, we would be in their hands.
So, we need well-established policies and the capacity to apply them, for the benefit of the Canadian farmers. As I said earlier, Madam Speaker, the present policies are effective. We would of course have to call upon people from the industry, the UPA for example, which represents our farm producers in Quebec. They have expressed their concerns during the meetings I had with them. They insisted that the government should not reduce at all the assistance it is providing them. That, of course, is their main request.
Since the commercial dairy farmers are already getting 5 per cent less for their milk, the slightest cutback will make farm relief even harder to find. As you know, the level of farm relief in Quebec-I cannot talk for the rest of the country-is extremely low. How do you expect the sons of farmers to follow in their fathers' steps if it means getting $250,000; $300,000 and up to $600,000 into dept? There is a provincial farmers assistance program I dealt with for many years. Generally speaking however, it is a heavy burden very few people are willing to support. Therefore, it is important to think about the future.
I do not want to do a historic retrospective but it is interesting to note that, 20 years ago, continuity was not a problem. Farmers' sons succeeded their fathers, which led to a very stable local economy. Farmers might have enjoyed stability but they had to work very hard to maintain their standard of living.
At the turn of the century, almost 70 per cent of our population lived in rural areas and over 25 per cent of our labour force worked the land. It is a high proportion. However, after the rapid industrialization that followed the First World War, this percentage fell to 15 per cent. Today, after World War II and the mechanization of agriculture, only 3 per cent of our labour force work the land. They have become very efficient and, with the new machinery and technology, it is obvious that our needs are enormous. But there are a lot more indirect jobs today me must take into account. For instance, in Ontario and Quebec, one out of seven jobs is directly or indirectly related to the agri-food industry.
To get to the point, Madam Speaker, if we cannot ensure the future, it is because present-day farmers did not get the help they so desperately need. We have lost some ground in the GATT negotiations and the Free Trade Agreement. It is very important that the government realizes there is a limit to what our farmers can handle.
If we loose our would-be farmers at that rate, you will see multinationals step in and take over the food-production industry, and that will spell the end of price stabilization. You can rest assured, Madam Speaker, that food prices will go up because, with those big multinationals, it is what the market can bear that counts, so to speak. But it is important for the government and the producers, UPA especially, who are watching closely the GATT negotiations and free trade. There is a potential danger for Canada to give in to American demands, especially when it comes to reducing the support given to our producers. It is extremely important that we maintain our security net for our farmers. If we do not, not

only will our farmers suffer, but it may also give rise to a social problem. Even if the population is concentrated in big cities, there are still people who want to farm. We must not take for granted that we can reduce the importance of farmers in our economy.
On the whole, I am sure that the government knows that UPA is watching it, and it is extremely important that it contacts the people concerned to make sure that the well-being of our farmers and of our food-producing industry is considered on the same footing as our National Defence.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Any questions or comments? Resuming debate. The hon. member for Stormont- Dundas.

Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak today on this very important motion which concerns the integrity and future stability of the Canadian agricultural industry.
I wish to commend my colleague, the member for Haldimand-Norfolk, for bringing this motion forward. I believe it is a timely motion in view of the impending deadline of the GATT negotiations in Geneva and also for its support in maintaining an economically viable and productive Canadian agricultural industry in which both our farmers and the Canadian consumers are the beneficiaries.
The motion urges the federal government within the GATT talks and its domestic economic policies to recognize the vital role of farmers in maintaining the Canadian way of life. It specifically calls upon the government to uphold the principles of Canada's supply management system and maintain agricultural safety net programs which provide stability and an equitable return for every sector involved in food production.
Supply
The motion also urges the government to adopt policies which promote sustainable development in farming as well as recognize the essential role of agricultural communities in our economy and the well-being of Canadians from coast to coast.
Canadians are aware of the importance of agriculture to our economy. A decline in productivity and stability of our agricultural sector would certainly have a negative impact on the country. The government must realize that a failure to adequately protect Canadian agriculture at GATT and within its own agricultural policies would be detrimental to every Canadian and have serious consequences for Canada's over-all economy.
For 15 years Canadian farmers have relied upon the supply management system to promote stability within agriculture and to obtain a reasonable return for their business. One sector of Canadian agriculture with a considerable interest in the GATT negotiations and which is dependent upon supply management is the dairy industry. There are over 34,000 dairy farms in Canada with some 70,000 farm families deriving their livelihood from this industry. For these people, marketing boards have to remain strong.
In addition, there are roughly 25,000 Canadians employed in the dairy processing industry working in 400 plants across Canada. The total figure of those involved in this one agricultural industry is close to 100,000 and represents approximately 14 per cent of the total Canadian agribusiness employment. When these figures are incorporated into figures for the other agricultural sector, one can see the importance of agriculture to our economy and to employment in Canada. Jobs are scarce in rural Canada and agriculture is the backbone of our rural communities.
The dairy farmers of Canada desire to retain the marketing boards and the supply management system in order to earn a living from the price they can charge for milk. Farmers do not take advantage of the consumer by inflating the cost of milk and other dairy products. They simply obtain a fair price for their products based on their input costs. Supply management accomplishes just that. Without such a system Canadian dairy, chicken and egg producers would not be able to continue in operation. Very few businesses could if it cost more to produce a product than what it sold for in the marketplace.

November 2, 1990
Supply
Canadians witness every day the quality of agricultural products our fanners produce. Most Canadians agree that Canada has established in a relatively short period of time an agricultural system that is envied by the rest of the world.
In my riding of Stormont-Dundas I have over 2,600 constituents involved in agriculture and related services industry. Among them are, in my unbiased opinion, some of the finest dairy, egg and chicken producers in the country. I also take great pleasure in the fact that at the Ault Foods plant in Winchester some of the finest cheese in the world is manufactured and they are recognized internationally for their products.
Our agricultural sector must continue to meet the high standards of quality we have in Canada today. It must also be able to continue in meeting the needs of our farmers and all Canadians.
A recent public opinion poll found that 94 per cent of Canadians believe it is important for the dairy industry to be self-sufficient. Eight-six per cent of respondents thought our dairy farmers were doing an excellent job and 70 per cent said that all the dairy products consumed in Canada can and should be produced in our country. Only 3 per cent thought that dairy farmers were overpaid, while 45 per cent believed they were underpaid. Consumers who were aware of milk marketing boards viewed them positively and said that they were beneficial to both the consumer and the producer.
Canadians also recognize the valuable contribution farmers have made to Canada's cultural and historical heritage. Farmers have worked the rural landscape for generations and the rural way of life is an integral component in our country's traditions. Our diverse climate affords farmers a shorter growing season, but they have nonetheless succeeded in providing the food needs of our country.
Today, however, high interest rates, rising input costs and uncertainty over the future of agriculture in Canada are combining to place increasing pressures on the ability of our farmers to survive. The concerns about supply management and the various safety net programs have added to these burdens. The federal government for its
part has yet to provide the kind of reassurances our agriculture community deserves.
The uncertainty over the outcome of the GATT talks in December has already caused problems for farmers in terms of their ability to obtain bank loans. Mr. Cyrille Parent, who chaired the annual conference on banking and agriculture held this month in Saint-Hyacinthe, Quebec, has stated that banks "are advising farmers not to take out loans for the next month". Banks themselves are quite concerned as well about the future of Canadian agriculture. They have a vested interest in the agricultural sector and its future viability.
In the last five years Canadian banks have written off over $560 million in bad loans and currently have $7.4 billion in outstanding loans to farmers. Obviously, our banks support the maintenance of supply management and the quota system in Canadian agriculture. They want to see this government take the appropriate action to support our farmers. They want to see Canadian farmers survive and continue their business relationship with the banking community.
Canadian farmers are not afraid of competing with the major agricultural nations of the world. What they simply want, however, is a fighting chance. They need the ability to compete and survive. Farmers realize the world is changing. They know that the agricultural trade issue is a major aspect of success of the GATT talks. No Canadian farmer wants to see a global war in agriculture, nor increased protectionist measures. Farmers recognize that if, for example, farm subsidies are to be phased out, then it must be done so in every country.
A level playing field must, however, exist in agriculture on the international scene. The United States is calling for the elimination of agricultural subsidies at the GATT. Yet the U.S. dairy producers are subsidized with U.S. government tax dollars. The U.S. farmer clearly admires the Canadian supply management system, so much so, that 11 of the major milk-producing states in the United States, which account for 80 per cent of production, implemented a system of production management on November 1 of this year. One therefore questions the actual commitment the U.S. government has to eliminating agricultural subsidies.

Canadian farmers are already at a disadvantage with their U.S. counterparts. Interest rates are lower in the U.S., and fuel costs, fertilizer costs, feed prices, and machinery parts are also lower in the U.S. than in Canada. There is little chance that our farmers would be able to compete with supply management if our safety net programs were entirely dismantled at the GATT.
Therefore, the federal government must stand steadfast in supporting our farmers. Prices for commodities have to reflect the costs Canadian farmers incur to produce their goods. Supply management has consistently provided a sufficient supply with a reasonable return for the farmer. The system works to protect the farmer and the consumer by tying prices to the average costs incurred by the most efficient producers and limiting production to estimates of domestic consumption. Thus, Canadians obtain a stable supply at fair prices. Without supply management, this relationship would end and so would Canadian agriculture.
In an editorial on October 30, 1990, The Ottawa Citizen discussed the need for international agricultural reform and the elimination of inefficiency in agriculture. However, it is also said that Canada should not give away the farm. The article pointed out that the Canadian consumer may well rejoice if, as a result of marketing boards being eliminated, the price of chicken fell. The article quickly noted, however, that the consumer would be less satisfied if market forces pushed the price of a drumstick beyond the budget of an average income family.
In conclusion, I have concentrated my remarks on the issue of supply management. I did so because I believe its future is interconnected to the future of agriculture in Canada. The federal government has both a moral duty and a responsibility to preserve the Canadian family farm and the rural landscape of Canada. It has the even greater task of protecting our economy and the welfare of Canadians. In the final analysis, whatever happens at GATT, Canadians will not forgive this government, should it relegate Canadian agriculture to a shadow of its historical past, and its present contribution to the wellbeing of our economy, our farmers, and our country.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the fact that the hon. member made his speech largely on the subject of supply management. However, I would like to ask him a question pertaining to some of the other aspects of the GATT negotiation process and Canadian agriculture.
It is no secret that the Liberal Party, which he represents, has had trouble winning seats in western Canada through the years, and there are lots of reasons for that. One reason given by the farm community was that the Liberal Party was seen as one of the forces which undermined the historic Crow rate for the movement of Canadian grain.
With the changes that were made under the Western Grain Transportation Act, the system was somewhat changed, but the principle of paying the railroads rather than paying the producers was maintained. However, now we see a situation, both in the GATT negotiations and in the task force report, where a process is under way to dramatically change the regime by which the Crow benefit is distributed and farmers fear it will be eliminated completely. This clearly seems to be the long-term agenda of the bureaucrats of the Departments of Transport and Agriculture and supported by two successive governments.
I appreciate that the hon. member is not a westerner, but I was wondering what the position of the Liberal Party is on this very important question, arising from the GATT and the task force. Does the Liberal Party support a continuation of paying the railways under the Crow or would the Liberal Party go along with the government's agenda to make some dramatic changes to that?

Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague from the New Democratic Party for his question. I am glad that he also recognized that being a member from eastern Ontario, I will not pretend to my colleagues in this Chamber, or to Canadian farmers whom we are discussing today, that the issue of the Crow rate, which you mentioned as being a western issue, is something on which I would say I am an expert.
I certainly think it merits a close review, but I think it is another of those issues which across the country has created a tremendous amount of anxiety in the farming community.

Supply
Although I welcome the question I certainly recognize I cannot answer it to your satisfaction. Farming is a serious issue, and I know all members taking part today recognize that fact. I will not speak to it, not being well versed on it, but certainly I recognize it is an issue of great concern to people in western Canada and the farming community. It is one of those items that is causing a tremendous amount of anxiety for our farming community. I certainly would hope that the government and all members would look at it very closely.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am in a statesmanlike mood today.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Are you? That's nice.

I am very pleased to see that the subject of the MTN negotiations of the Uruguay round is being debated in the House. The Liberal opposition, I believe, introduced this motion and they should be congratulated on at last, after four years, showing some interest in this subject.
I am happy to be able to say that I can find nothing offensive in this resolution that we are debating. This is most unusual. This is the first time I have ever looked at a Liberal resolution and found nothing offensive in it.
Time for you to sit down then.

What the House urges is that in the GATT negotiations and in our economic policies, we recognize the essential role played by farmers in maintaining the Canadian way of life. There's certainly no question about that. It is a central feature of our policy.
It urges the government to uphold the principles of supply management. Madam Speaker, ever since we assumed office, we have been assuring and reassuring the Canadian farmer who is involved in the supply management farming industries that we intend to uphold the principles of supply management. This is exactly what we have done in our offer tabled in the first half of October at Geneva in complying with our obligations in the MTN negotiations. We are doing that.
Then it urges us to maintain the safety nets to provide a stable and fair return for till sectors involved in food production, another central feature of our policy. As a matter of fact the Minister of Agriculture at present has
a major study under way in co-operation with all facets of the farming industry to ensure policies and principles to provide for a stable and fair return in all of those sectors.
It urges us to adopt policies encouraging sustainable development of farming practices-that is a given-and to recognize the vital role played by agricultural communities in the over-all economy and the well-being of all Canadians, which is another well-recognized principle to which we subscribe.
This is a resolution which we can support without any difficulty.
Madam Speaker, I believe that the Uruguay round of the multilateral trade negotiations is the most important single economic decision-making event that will take place in the 1990s-or at least as far as one can see ahead in the 1990s. There is no more important set of economic events being decided than the Uruguay round, which is going to conclude in the first week of December in Brussels, after a four-year period of intensive negotiation on 15 subjects.
I have not the time to go into all 15 subjects of course today, and we are mainly interested in agriculture this afternoon. But one of the most important sectors of the 15 being discussed-the most important I think it is fair to say-is the agricultural sector.
It is widely agreed by those participating in the negotiations that, unless there is a satisfactory resolution of the agricultural issues, there will be no satisfactory ending to the Uruguay round in December in Brussels. In other words, some of the more important trading nations involved in these discussions, including the United States and all members of the Cairns Group and I think most of the representatives of developing world, are determined that agriculture is to be brought under the system of GATT rules so that some principles of fairness and equity apply in the world agricultural trading sector, which is not now the case.
There have been efforts in the past to deal with agricultural trade, but they have been largely unsuccessful in dealing with non-tariff import barriers and the question of subsidies, and in particular export subsidies.
Many areas of agriculture are not subject to effective GATT rules at all.
As we all know, the United States has had a waiver in many of these areas since 1954 or 1955. The offer we have made in the GATT negotiations, of course, is subject to all of this being removed. We will not sustain our offer, for example, if there was any suggestion that the waiver the United States now has is to continue in the future. Our offer is made subject to certain conditions being met.
What is our offer? It is an initial and conditional offer, conditional on other countries agreeing to negotiate a substantial agricultural trade reform package with concrete benefits for our own agriculture. It is designed to achieve, over a 10-year period, an end to the international subsidy war through total elimination and prohibition of export subsidies. That is the first objective.
It is sad to report that as of today, November 2, the European Community has found itself unable to agree on any proposal to table at Geneva with reference to agriculture, despite the agreement of all the countries involved in these negotiations that by October 15 every country should table its offer on agriculture. As at November 2, the European Community is unable to table any offer.
An offer that was proposed by Mr. MacSharry, Commissioner of Agriculture for the European Community, I think about two months ago and was found to be totally inadequate by the United States, ourselves, and other members of the Cairns Group. It amounted to perhaps a 30 per cent reduction in trade distorting support for agriculture over a base period that started in 1986. In effect, they were only proposing a 13 per cent to 17 per cent reduction in subsidies for agriculture.
Everyone involved, except the European Community, agreed that that offer was totally unsatisfactory and it has not been agreed to by even the 12 members of the European Community. Germany and France, in particular, have refused to approve even that kind of an inadequate offer by the European Community,. The result is that the result that the European Community is going to meet again on Monday to decide whether they will approve an offer at all.
Supply
It is quite obvious, if the European Community does not come up with an offer shortly, at least something that can be discussed, that the whole structure of these MTN discussions may collapse. The European Community, if not the most powerful economic block in the world, is certainly one the of the two leading economic powers of the world. If the EC does not produce some kind of an offer shortly, then this is affecting negotiations in the other 14 sectors.
I presume the morale of the people involved is starting to disappear because they all know what I and anyone who studies this subject knows that, if there is not some kind of progress in agriculture, there will be no progress in any of those areas. If there is a failure of this round, I envisage that the 1990s are going to be much more difficult for every country involved in the world trading system than may already be projected.
A failure of these negotiations will result in trade chaos, the formation of trade blocs, in hurricane-like increases, and protectionist devices. We have already seen all kinds of resort to protectionist devices in various parts of the world, including the United States, the world's most important market. There will be a hurricane-like increase if these talks fail. There will be a tremendous increase in unilateral action or unilateralism as it is known in the MTN.
There will be a tremendous increase in bully-boy tactics by the giants of the world economic and trading system who, of course, if unrestrained by rules, are going to exert their influence through raw economic power. That is why, Madam Speaker, it is so important to us that we have a successful conclusion to this round. When the battle that depends simply on raw economic power commences, then we are not among the leading nations of the world in that respect. We are a middle-ranking nation. We are an importing trading nation, far beyond our size. One-third of our GNP is dependent upon trade, so we are very dependent for our prosperity on a properly functioning world trading system with clearly recognized rules that we can appeal to when the giants attempt to bully us around. That is the importance of the new rule-making system which we are having great success with and with the new system that would apply if this round is successful with reference to the acceptance and enforcement of panels. A lot of progress has been

Supply
made in those areas which is why we must settle this thorny issue of agriculture.
With respect to our own agricultural offer which I referred to, one objective is the question of export subsidies. One of the difficulties with the European Community is that the European Community appears determined not to agree to any restrictions with respect to export subsidies. If the European Community is not going to agree to any restriction on its right to give the tremendous export subsidies it is now giving its grain and other farmers, then Canada is going to continue to be savaged in the competition between the EC, the U.S., and others through the use of export subsidies. That is one objective.
The second objective is greater market orientation through a reduction of up to 50 per cent in trade distorting, internal subsidies, combined with clearer rules on what is to constitute non-countervailable or non-trade distorting support for agriculture. This is most important.
It is not all internal subsidies, Madam Speaker. It is trade distorting internal subsidies and clear rules. What kind of support can you give which will not be subject to countervail and will be non-trade distorting? That is to be decided in this round, some clear rules on those subjects.
Our third objective is improved market access through a one-third reduction of normal tariffs, resulting on bound rates no higher than 20 per cent.
The final, major objective is greater security for supply management through a strengthened and clarified Article XI of the GATT, in accordance with the proposal we made in March of this year, and which would include minimum market access levels pursuant to our international obligations.
A strengthened and clarified Article XI is needed if our dairy farmers are to be properly protected with the supply management system we now have. They know and understand that. The status quo will not adequately protect Canadian dairy farmers today. That is why it is so important that we reach success in these negotiations. That is an additional reason. Without a strengthened and clarified Article XI, a GATT panel has already indicated that dairy farmers are going to be in difficulty as a result of an interpretation of the present rules of the GATT.
With respect to minimum market access levels, all that has been suggested is that, over a 10-year period, the minimum market access levels with respect to supply management programs would increase to 5 per cent of the domestic market. I do not have the time to go into detail and I think all members are familiar with it. It has had a good reception.
The hon. member referred to the The Ottawa Citizen editorial of October 30. It states:
As such, the Canadian government's bargaining position on
agricultural trade in the multilateral trade talks now underway makes
good sense.
That is the opinion of the editorial writers of The Ottawa Citizen.
There has been criticism from some of the representatives of the dairy industry, although they have been muted in their criticism compared to the kind of protest they can make when they are really upset about a particular issue. Naturally, in their public statements, they are going to put forward what appears to be a perfect position for the dairy farmers, just as the brewery workers would put forward what would be a perfect position for them, or the beef cattle farmers for them, or the fishermen for them. They would like perfection, but they know that perfection is not possible in the world that we live in. One must accept trade-offs and compromises so long as they are ones that leave fundamental principles still protected.
There is widespread support of the fact that we have been able to put in an offer which is good for both of the main sectors of our farming industry: the farm exporting interests in grain, beef cattle, pork, and the like, which are very badly damaged at the present time by export subsidies; and the supply management sector, such as dairy and poultry products in particular, which are the beneficiaries of our supply management system and who want it to be continued in the future, just as the government wants it to be continued in the future.
I can quote the October 23, 1990 release of the Canadian Cattlemen's Association which states that our offer is "a good start to a more balanced world in which to trade". It has stated that it is a well balanced offer.
Mr. Albert Chambers of the Canadian Chicken Marketing Agency, on October 16, 1990 said:
November 2, 1990

Poultry and egg producers would have little or nothing to complain
about.
Mr. Knoerr of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, on October 16, 1990, said the national farm group "strongly supports the main thrust of the proposals" in an article in The Ottawa Citizen.
On October 16, 1990, a press release from Dairy Farmers of Canada, with regard to Article XI stated:
-the position tabled by the federal government is fully supportive of the recommendation of Dairy Farmers of Canada.
The Quebec government issued a press release quite supportive of our position. Even the UPA and the Co-op Federee de Quebec thought that our offer was a positive evolution. They have areas of concern but generally speaking, they have been positive and the Quebec government has been supportive.
We are off to a good start insofar as our position is concerned. The United States has made a proposal which would go further than ours with reference to export subsidies. As I say, the European Community does not even want to discuss the elimination or any reduction in import subsidy levels at all. One can see that there is still a tremendous gap in the positions of those who have to reach an agreement within five weeks.
The government is providing unprecedented support to our farmers. Between 1984 and 1989, direct and indirect federal expenditures in the agricultural sector totalled about $22 billion. Some $12 billion has gone to hard-pressed grain, that is, the grain and oilseed sectors, to compensate for the low prices caused by the subsidy war. That was one of the main items, but $22 billion altogether. This is certainly more than adequate proof that the principles expressed in this resolution had been accepted and acted on by the government.
The price tag of this trade war is tremendously high world-wide. The OECD showed in 1989 the member countries of the OECD spent $245 billion U.S. in transfers to agriculture. In the European Community it was $90 billion just about; in the U.S., $66.6 billion; Japan, $59 billion and in that same year in Canada we spent $7 billion.
As a trading nation, we cannot afford to have this kind of war continuing. It is not a war that we can win. Fifty
Supply
per cent of our total agriculture receipts come from export trade. That dependence is most crucial in the grains and oilseeds sector where 70 to 80 per cent of receipts come from their exports. That is why in our offer we have tried to be balanced and comprehensive, to achieve both long term benefits for our export industries and long term benefits for our farming industries that come under supply management.
If we can have this position of ours accepted in the next five weeks, there will have been a major step forward for Canada both respect to our economic health generally and the economic health of the Canadian farming community. I would certainly be glad of any support that members of the House on all sides can give to our success in trying to get the fundamentals of this offer accepted by the other countries involved.

Madam Speaker, I listened carefully to the Minister when he referred to a letter from the Quebec farmers union supporting the Canadian government's representations on their behalf.
I would like to ask the Minister whether he quoted exactly what the President of the Quebec farmers union said in his letter. I had the opportunity, in the last few days, to meet him at the Belanger-Campeau Commission in Quebec and he was absolutely furious and insulted at having been misquoted in this House by the Minister of State for Agriculture, the hon. member for Montmagny. In reply to harsh criticism by opposition members, the Minister defended himself by saying that Mr. Proulx, the President of the Quebec farmers union, wrote in a letter that the union approved the government's action when, in fact, he repeated their concerns about the representations made by the Canadian government at the GATT which, if they do not succeed, can threaten the future of Quebec agriculture. The union has often wondered whether the government was acting in good faith at the GATT talks.
At other times, it questioned the objectivity and even the strategy of the Canadian negotiating team at the GATT, which it believes is clearly doomed to failure. Even if the Minister tries, in his report today in this House, to make us believe his representations will

Supply
succeed, the harsh reality is that they probably will not bring about the protection demanded by the farmers.
So it is one thing to tell the minister, yes, we hope you will succeed and that farm support programs will remain. But it is something else again to see the government really get ahead at the GATT negotiations in ensuring the protection farmers want and we wish on this side of the House of Commons.
So when the minister quotes a letter from the Quebec association, UPA, I would appreciate it if he would report exactly what was said and not leave the impression he got a blank cheque from the Union, when in fact they express strong reservations about the Canadian government's initiative at the GATT negotiations.

Madam Speaker I have not quoted any letter from the UPA. If the hon. gentleman had listened to me attentively as he should have, he would have heard me say that the joint press release by Mr. Prolix and Mr. Pelletier was generally positive. I said that the two presidents saw our Canadian offer as a positive evolution. I went on to say, of course they did not approve the total offer. There were some areas of criticism by them. I explained how, even if your offer was perfect, it would never be perfect enough to get the full support of the group in question because they are looking for perfection and they want 100 per cent in a world where you are never going to get 100 per cent.
I do not want to repeat all of that, but generally speaking their reaction has been moderate and positive. That is my interpretation. There are certain things they do not like as well. They do not like the 5 per cent minimal access level proposed for the dairy sector over 10 years. If all our other objectives are achieved and the rest of the world does away with the inequitable situation that now exists and the United States does away with its waiver and we are successful over 10 years, we would give a 5 per cent minimal access level for the dairy sector. They do not like that.
How are we to achieve any of these objectives if we are not prepared to give anywhere? They are not the negotiators. The do not have the responsibility, so they can be out there representing their pressure group as
lobbyists and, of course, demand perfection, knowing that if they were in our shoes they would have to do exactly the same. You have to give something to get something.
We cannot say to the rest of the world: "Recognize supply management, strengthen the wording as we want it strengthened in article XI(2)(1) and do what we want in that area, but we are not going to give you any increased access at all, even over the next 10 years, no matter what you do with respect to the dairy sector". No one in the rest of the world is going to buy that. Our provision here is reasonable, but they say they do not agree with it. I cannot criticize them for taking the absolute position on behalf of their clients. What else would you expect them to take? I have nothing to apologize for. I think I have described quite correctly the situation.
There is a negotiation on, and unless Canada is not to participate, unless we are to say that we, as one of the 100 nations that belong to GATT, are not going to engage in this negotiation, then we have got to take risks. Those who are worried about what the results may be will just have to wait and see.
We already have a position in agriculture, supported right across this country despite the many conflicting interests in the agricultural and farming community across this country, and we have a couple of very brilliant negotiators in charge of this, Mr. Germain Denis, who is in charge of our MTN negotiations under the supervision of Gerry Shannon, the former deputy minister, Mr. Mike Gifford, and others from the Department of Agriculture.
We have the assistance of the Minister of Agriculture, whom I hope to have in Brussels with me during the final week, as well as the Minister of State for Agriculture who is very attentive on behalf of the Quebec farmer.

We also have the Minister of State for Agriculture, the minister in charge of the Wheat Board. I am going to have lots of help. I have no doubt I will be under intense surveillance.
