As should rightly be the case.

We are aware that Mr. Proulx does not approve 100 per cent of what we are doing. I think we would be hearing a lot more from him if basically they did not think we were on the right track.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the tone of statesmanship which the minister has adopted here, and recognized that we do have a common interest in reducing the very vicious export subsidy war which has been going on.
However, the supply management sector in this country, I think, really is starting to feel like the black knight in the Monty Python movie that is losing one limb at a time and keeps trying to dance on the road as his limbs disappear.
Certainly, the effect of free trade and the opening up of the imports into the supply management sector is becoming more and more clear.
Right up front, we are offering to increase imports under the GATT. This is creating pressure from our own processors in this country as well letting loose a real howl in the media: an attack on the supply management system.
I would like to ask the minister specifically why the Canadian government agreed to adopt a producers subsidy equivalent system of evaluating subsidies, because what it has done is to include the benefits of supply management, which are actually derived from the marketplace, and instead portray them as a subsidy not only in the trade negotiations but to our own public which is examining this and following this debate.
Why has the Canadian government taken that approach which very much distorts the picture? Second, why is the government putting the accrual benefit on the table at the GATT when in fact nobody is asking us to get rid of it, or to seriously alter it?

Madam Speaker, of course at the GATT, all measures of assistance in the agricultural field are being examined.
It was determined by the negotiating group on agriculture and its chairman that by October 1 each country would table its base line data on agriculture. The answer had to be prepared following guidelines that the chairman defined. Of course, that is what we did. That is
Supply
without prejudice as to whether or not we agree with these particular guidelines. We do not, and we have made that clear, of them we agree with. Some of them we do not agree with. That was clearly stated when we submitted the data, and I quote: "It is without prejudice to the negotiating positions of the participants or to the outcome of the negotiations." There will be a whole negotiation on qualifications, conditions, what is a trade distorting subsidy, what is not, what is a green measure and what is a non-green measure.
We are not at all prejudiced in our approach by responding with the information requested by the chairman of the negotiating committee.
On the Crow benefit, that will have to be examined like every other program of assistance in the agricultural field to see if it is a green measure or a non-green measure. Some of it might be green and some of it might be non-green.
If it has to be changed in any way, the benefit will continue. We are committed to the Crow benefit as a historic benefit to the agri-food industry on the prairies. We are committed that the benefit will continue, but how the benefit is delivered is open for discussion here and in Geneva. If one way of delivering it is agreed to be trade distorting, we will find another way to deliver it. The benefit itself is going to be continued, although the method of delivering it might have to be changed, depending on the outcome of these negotiations. I think that is clear enough.

Madam Speaker, in part the motion before the House reads:
Thai this House urge that in the upcoming GATT negotiations and in over-all economic policies, the government recognize the essential role played by farmers in maintaining the Canadian way of life-
I think that it is an excellent motion and that the tenor of debate in support of the motion in the House today from all parties, I might add, is heartening indeed.
At the outset I want to say that my colleagues and I in the New Democratic Party opposition certainly give our full support to the Minister of Agriculture and to the

Supply
Minister for International Trade in the very difficult role they have to play in these upcoming GATT negotiations.
We recognize the fact that we are playing in many respects in a global agricultural marketplace and that certain concessions have to be made. It is a difficult role. I understand that there are many pressures from all sectors of the agricultural community in terms of preserving what they perceive to be necessaiy structures and necessary supports in order to ensure the continued vitality of the industry.
However, we do have some concerns with regard to perhaps matters of interpretation and matters of definition and what constitutes an unfair trade subsidy or a distorting trade subsidy. We have some concerns, quite frankly, about the fact that Canada in many ways seems to be between a rock and a hard place with respect to the negotiations going on in GATT, the severe pressure put upon Canada by its U.S. neighbour, and the situation that we face with countervailable sanctions through the free trade agreement.
I would like to go into some of those arguments and try as best I can to put into perspective some of those concerns. However, before I do, I would like to give a brief perspective in terms of the nature of the industry that we are actually dealing with in Canada. Many Canadians do not really recognize the importance of the agricultural industry to our economy and to our way of life.
Today there are about 35,000 dairy farms in Canada, with each farm supporting at least two families. There are about 25,000 Canadians working in the dairy industry in about 400 plants right across the country. Speaking specifically of the dairy industry, we produce about 7.6 billion litres of milk annually. Dairy farming in Canada, as only one sector of our agricultural community, represents close to $3.8 billion in farm sales and contributes a significant portion to our Gross Domestic Product, about $7 billion.
That is only one sector of our agricultural community, a very important sector and a sector which I submit may be significantly affected by the decisions made either through GATT or by the bilateral panel on negotiations through the free trade agreement.
One thing that is very clear to all members of the House is that we do have a growing crisis in agriculture. We can talk about the grain lying in the field in Saskatchewan, because although we have record harvests we cannot sell it. This is a direct result of the devastating export subsidy warfare that has been promulgated by the United States and the European Community. Quite frankly Canadian agriculture has been left in tatters as a result of that warfare.
There is no question. I totally agree with the minister that we have to try to eliminate those unfair export subsidy concessions. Frankly we cannot play in that kind of ball game. We do not have the productive capacity or the economic capacity to be able to sustain that kind of an economic onslaught.
We have a problem in agriculture in Canada. It is a crisis that has been deepening since 1984. In one year alone, 1987-1988, we lost 24,000 jobs in our agricultural community. The farm debt in Canada now exceeds some $22 billion according to 1989 figures. Independent of what sector of the agricultural community they work in, about one-third of all farmers are facing very serious debt and the possibility of bankruptcy. Many of them are on the verge of bankruptcy or have gone bankrupt. One out of five farmers on family farms in Canada are living in virtual poverty.
Those are very sobering figures which certainly bring into question the kinds of policies followed over the last eight or ten years in terms of the commitment this institution must make to our agricultural community.
In 1961, just about 30 years ago, we had 480,000 farms in Canada. But, as of 1986, that number was reduced to less than 293,000 viable farms. That is a staggering loss in that economic sector. As a result, our rural communities are losing a very important economic base. They are losing a way of life. That is most disturbing.
We have seen an alarming trend developing as a result of the policies of this administration, a trend that favours the free market agenda, the corporate agenda, bowing to the shrine of the global free marketplace. We have seen the cancellation of farm subsidies; the abolition of interest-free loans; an increase in the federal surtax on agricultural goods; and high interest rates, which of
November 2, 1990

course have been most devastating to our farmers, particularly younger farmers who have had to carry a high debt load getting into the business and trying to expand their operations.
We have seen the impact of outrageous exchange rates between Canada and the U.S. and the difficulties that has created, not only in agriculture but in virtually all export sectors. With the 7 per cent goods and services tax, all of these things are adding up to some very difficult times indeed for our agricultural communities.
We have seen a slow capitulation of this government to repeated U.S. demands to reduce market support mechanisms in agriculture. That was enshrined in the free trade agreement that is now into its second year.
I just want to read Article 701 of the free trade agreement signed by both countries, regarding agricultural subsidies:
The Parlies agree that their primary goal with respect to agricultural subsidies is to achieve, on a global basis, the elimination of all subsidies which distort agricultural trade, and the Parties agree to work together to achieve this goal,
That sounds very honourable. On the surface I do not think most people would find much to object to, except when you try to determine what this definition of a "market distorting subsidy" actually implies. We get into difficulty there because we see that Canada's marketing board structure has been fingered by the United States agribusiness sector as a trade distorting subsidy. That is a challenge they submitted previous to this. If that means that Canada is committed through this agreement to eliminating that kind of a "trade distorting subsidy", it spells real problems for our farmers and particularly for our dairy farmers.
If the United States fails to secure the reductions in terms of internal subsidies through the current Uruguay Round of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, the GATT negotiations we have been talking about, it will likely continue to go after Canadian marketing boards through the bilateral dispute settlement mechanism under the free trade agreement. If it does not get us in GATT, it will likely attempt to get us through the FTA.
Supply
I want to read from another article in the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. This section is Article 703, "Market Access for Agriculture". It reads:
In order to facilitate trade in agricultural goods, the Parties shall
work together to improve access to each other's markets through the
elimination or reduction of import barriers.
We are looking at a statement which basically says to open up the process to give opportunity for improved access to each other's markets.
When we think of it in terms of the capacity of the U.S. agricultural industry and the small capacity of the Canadian industry in perspective, what that may very well lead to is a virtual swamping of our Canadian markets with cheap U.S. agricultural goods.
We have already seen a virtual exodus on a daily basis of consumers in border towns across Canada leaving Canada to go shopping down in the United States to pick up dairy products, cheap gasoline and then come back into Canada. We cannot blame people for trying to find the best value for their dollar, but I am sure that when Canadian shoppers go down to the United States to spend their millions of dollars daily in its markets picking up those cheaper products, they are not thinking about the impact it has on our own agricultural industry and dairy sector, how it affects the jobs in that sector or how it affects our tax base. I certainly do not blame them for trying to find good value, but it is having a devastating effect on our own domestic economies.
If we open up our borders in that respect and guarantee a freer access, we are going to be running into some very difficult times in terms of the restructuring of the agricultural industry in Canada because of competition with U.S. products.
We could well become, I submit, a dumping ground for the excess U.S. capacity because the system down there is a little different. They do not control production. They subsidize the cost of production and can run into very large excesses of dairy products, for example butter which has to be dumped somewhere. What a convenient dumping ground it would be to have Canadian borders open and free to accept those products.
The Macdonald Commission which was struck sometime ago, before the free trade agreement was brought into effect, recommended that agriculture as an economic sector be excluded from the free trade agreement. As a matter of fact, as we all know, history has written that

Supply
this government ignored that recommendation and included agriculture as an important component in the FTA.
Through that, the United States won some major concessions. It won the reduction of the powers of the Canadian Wheat Board. It won the removal of transportation subsidies in Canada. It won the phase-out of tariffs. It won on a number of fronts.
To give a good example of the almost immediate overnight impact of the free trade agreement in terms of Canadian agriculture, it was the grape growing industry, particularly in British Columbia, involving virtually thousands of acres of prime agricultural grape growing. Virtually the grapes were tom out of the ground and the land was left to lay fallow because the industry could not compete with the changes brought about by the free trade agreement. It is true that there has been somewhat of a comeback in certain grape varieties, but certainly it is not the vibrant industry it was before the free trade agreement came into effect.
In many ways our agricultural markets may simply become niche markets that will supply specialty products but will not have the capacity that they should have to supply the Canadian consumer with Canadian products.
Having won those concessions through the free trade agreement, I submit that the U.S. is now intent on including the dairy industry in future negotiations. It essentially said that in the FTA, although dairy sort of escaped the first round of negotiations, they intend to include the dairy industry in any future rounds of negotiations. I ask, Madam Speaker, whether the inclusion of the Canadian dairy industry in future negotiations may be a possible precedent for Canada's participation in the trilateral negotiations that are now going on between the U.S., Mexico, and Canada, which has indicated that it wishes to participate. Is this going to be one of the concessions we have to make?
I want to point out, Madam Speaker, that the American farm bureau concluded that, with regard to the free trade agreement, once tariffs were removed American grains, bakery goods, poultry, eggs and milk products will gain substantial access to Canadian markets and undermine the marketing board system.
There is no question that our way of doing business in terms of Canadian agriculture is being jeopardized, not only by the free trade agreement, but also by the current negotiations that are taking place right now in the General Agreement on Thriffs and Trades.
I can recall back before I was elected, listening to one of the free trade policy advisers for the current minister of trade when they were out in the Okanagan. This gentleman was a specialist in agricultural negotiations and he was being pressed by the farmers pretty strongly as to why this government was committing agriculture to the free trade discussions. He said, and I wrote it down at the time: "When it comes right down to it, some things are more important politically than they are economically".
Madam Speaker, to me that says that this government at that time was willing to sacrifice the Canadian agricultural industry for political expediency. I think that is proving itself to be the case.
We have seen the phase-out of many of the controls and protections for our agricultural industry. If it continues unabated through GATT or through the FTA it could very well spell the demise of the industry. The truth of the matter is that-and we often hear this phrase touted-there has to be a level playing field, but there is no level playing field when it comes to agriculture.
There are a number of reasons. We are a northern climate and have a shorter growing season. It is more difficult and more costly for us to produce on a per-unit basis than, for example, a farmer in Florida or California. We have higher labour rates. The geography of the country and the fact that we are such a massive country with such a small population means that transportation costs are higher.
These factors mitigate against the concept of a level playing field, and make essential the necessity for certain market structures to continue to exist in the Canadian agricultural industry if it in fact wishes to survive.
The United States has basically been calling for free trade in agriculture. As I mentioned before, we have seen the devastating trade wars that are taking place between the United States and the European community. They have to stop. There is no question about it. We
November 2, 1990

support any measures that the government can implement in order to eliminate those trade wars.
At the same time I have to caution that in doing so, we cannot be entrapped into capitulating the future of our marketing boards in order to secure a negotiation.
The United States has been most vociferous in calling for the elimination of subsidization in the agriculture community. When we look at the U.S. system, we find that it is virtually awash in subsidies at the producer level. I would suggest to the Minister for International Trade and the Minister of Agriculture that if the United States wants to play ball in terms of eliminating international warfare in trade subsidies, they call upon the United States to remove the kind of market subsidies that are rampant in the U.S. industry.
Madam Speaker, I am going to skip over some of the other points that I had wanted to make, and in summary say that the members on this side of the House sympathize with the difficult position of the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister for International Trade when it comes to these international negotiations. We wish to see a successful conclusion of the negotiations, but we do not wish to see those negotiations meaning a capitulation of Canada's historical perspective in terms of its commitment to agriculture and its commitment to maintaining the market structures that are now in place.

Madam Speaker, the hon. member for Okanagan-Shuswap said-and I did check his remarks-that the goods and services tax would apply to the agricultural sector when in fact it will be exempted. Everybody knows that. He also said that the structures must remain in the agricultural sector.
I must say that the Minister of Agriculture met with Mr. Proulx of the Union des producteurs agricoles in Montreal and these people are satisfied with the way Canadian government officials are handling the negotiations. They are giving priority to GATT multilateral trade negotiations because they provide greater security for the supply management system by strengthening and clarifying GATT Article XI which covers minimum access to the Canadian market.
Supply
Unless I am mistaken, my colleague also spoke in favour of these GATT negotiations, so I have a question for him. Considering that for years now the Canadian agricultural sector has been one of the major beneficiaries of the export trade, and assuming he wants to maintain the markets we have with other countries, where does he think the Canadian government ought to put its priorities in the GATT negotiations?

Madam Speaker, I think the member raises some valid points. I am concerned with Canada's position in the GATT negotiations, because it is basically offering to open the door essentially to a phase-out of trade distorting subsidies. The essence of the problem is how do we define those trade distorting subsidies. Who is going to make that determination? In fact, as I have said earlier on, the United States has already fingered the concept of our marketing board structures as being such a subsidy.
We say that we are going to open the door, we are going to make these concessions by phasing out these kinds of structures, and at the same time, through Article XI we are trying to beef up the security for the marketing board structures. We are in a philosophical catch 22. On the one hand we are capitulating, and on the other hand we are saying that we need greater security through Article XI for our marketing boards.
The question is, how can we open it up on the one hand and then strengthen it on the other. That is the kind of philosophical quandary that this government finds itself in. There is no question that Canadian agriculture should be seeking to expand its markets, as the member had asked.
For example, when I was in South Korea last fall as part of an interparliamentary trade delegation, I found there were many opportunities, not only in the agricultural sector but also in our softwood lumber sector. These were opportunities for development of niche markets in the Pacific-Asia market area. This applies to Korea, in particular, because its economy is changing rapidly and very dynamically. We need an aggressive marketing presence for our agricultural commodities. We still have some difficulties with South Korea having its own tariff structures and, quite naturally, wanting to

November 2, 1990
Private Members' Business
protect its own industries. There are certainly opportunities there.
We must certainly look abroad. One of the difficulties I have with the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement is that it focuses on commerce between the two nations. We have no argument with the concept of freer trade, whether it be on a sectoral basis or on a general basis. The reduction of exposed tariff structures should be accommodated. At the same time, we should be looking at reducing those barriers as we are trying to do through GATT on a multilateral basis, so that we can expand our agricultural markets into those other areas rather than just focusing on the U.S. market.
When one looks at the capacity of the United States agricultural industry and looks at the capacity of the Canadian industry, it does not require a rocket scientist to figure out who is going to be the winner and who is going to be the loser.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to clarify the New Democratic Party's position on this subject. I felt they would always be supportive of the GATT as a body to help us establish world trading order. Is that the position of the New Democratic Party?
Also, do they not agree that if we could reduce, over a period of time, the trade distorting subsidies that are prevailing in many other countries of this world, then we could take part in the world marketplace much easier and much more successfully.

Madam Speaker, there is no argument from me on that account.
What does concern us is the definition of what constitutes a trade distorting subsidy. If the concept of our marketing board structures is inclusive in that definition, then I say we have gone too far. I do not think that we can dismantle the protective mechanisms that are necessary for controlled and efficient market system that we have developed in Canada. If our marketing board structures are part of that definition as a trade distorting subsidy, then we do not support that. But we do support the elimination of other trade distorting subsidies such as the production subsidies that are given to the U.S. market. When one looks at the U.S. market, many of their subsidies are hidden but they are there. The agriculture community in the United States is awash in subsidies. Those are trade distorting subsidies.
The export subsidy warfare that has been ongoing between the U.S. and the European Common Market has left Canadian agriculture, particularly our grains and oilseeds, in absolute tatters. Those subsidies have to be eliminated.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   THE ECONOMY SOCIAL OWNERSHIP
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   THE ECONOMY SOCIAL OWNERSHIP
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of protecting and extending the important role of social ownership in the economy, in order to achieve the social goals of full employment, regional equity, technological development and equality among Canadians.
He said: Madam Speaker, it is a very great pleasure to move this motion to protect and extend the important role of social ownership in the economy which we certainly see in our party as something that is critical to achieving broader social goals of full employment, regional equity, technological development, and equality among Canadians.
Traditionally, when people consider the question of social ownership, they may think that we are hearkening back to the past ideological debates of the 1930s, 1940s and the 1950s; ideological debates which equated social ownership with what we usually call Crown corporations or public ownership. That is an interesting ideological debate. One can certainly make the case, and I would not try to undercut it, that historically Crown corporations have been extremely crucial to our development as a nation. We can see that with respect to everything from the railways back in the 1800s to Petro-Canada in the present day.
It is not that notion or view of social ownership that I want to talk about in the context of this motion. Instead, I want to talk about social ownership as community-based ownership. I want to talk particularly about institutions such as co-operatives and credit unions, and some of the new developments in co-operatives which are not just consumer purchasing co-operatives which have been so important for instance in the west in the past. As I
November 2, 1990

discuss this motion, I want to talk particularly about producer co-operatives, and, within that context, especially worker co-operatives.
If we take the context of co-operatives as a whole, there are perhaps as many as 12 million Canadians who are members of a co-operative or a credit union, or a caisse populaire in Quebec. That is nearly 43 per cent of adult Canadians. More than 60,000 people in fact are directly involved in directing a co-operative system through their activities as volunteer board members.
For instance, I am a member of a credit union and, partly because of my work here, I am not able to be a board member, but I count on the volunteer work of people whom I elect to direct that credit union. The same thing is true of producer co-operatives. The same thing is true of producer co-operatives. The same thing is true of consumer co-operatives right across the country. It is a tremendous area of economic activity which is, in fact, largely ignored in our economic debates.
When we consider that there are 43 per cent of Canadians who are part of this co-operative movement, it seems to me unfortunate that there is not more consideration given to the potential role which co-operatives and credit unions could play.
The total assets of Canadian co-operatives, including financial co-operatives, are $68 billion, so we are not talking about something marginal. We are not talking about something which is playing a very limited role in our economy. We are talking about important institutions which can be so much more important in the future.
For instance, credit unions and caisses populaires each year lend approximately $37 billion to their members. The annual revenues of non-financial co-operatives in fact are close to $15 billion. We have co-operatives in marketing. We have co-operatives in food, housing, day care, health care, communication, even funeral services, manufacturing, processing, and so forth.
These co-operatives have a long history in our country. What is exciting are the new challenges which have now been presented to our co-operative movement, which represent the new role that exists for this form of social ownership within our country.
Private Members' Business
For instance, Laird Hunter from the Canadian Co-operative Association testified last year to a parliamentary committee on Bill C-21. He indicated-this is an especially important point-that increasingly those interested in worker co-operative development are concerning themselves with the contribution that worker co-operative buy-outs might be able to make in plant shutdown situations. He went on to say: "Given the uncertain future of many sectors, Canada's manufacturing base, the Canadian Co-operative Association strongly believes that, as amendments are considered to legislation relevant to worker co-operative development, provisions facilitating the growth of worker co-operative sectors should be considered."
That is the thrust of my argument today. In the context of a recession and wide-spread plant shutdowns throughout the country, we have to recognize that there is a potential for workers if the legislation helps them and if the financial support is provided through institutions and through government to make it possible. It is not in all cases, and probably not even in most cases, but in a significant number of cases. There is the capacity for workers to be able to provide a response to the problems that plant shutdowns bring, not just to them personally, but to their communities.
Mr. Laird, in some of his comments went on to note that in looking at worker co-operatives at the present time, there are a great number of such initiatives in the Province of Quebec.

Many co-operatives in the province of Quebec exist to establish the feasibility of continuing to operate factories that are in trouble. In fact, the same principle can be applied in other sectors of our economy.

Mr. Laird suggested that one can see these initiatives in the delivery business. On the west coast, there are a number of instances in manufacturing. He said that, increasingly, the co-operative system as a whole is being asked for assistance with this kind of endeavour.

Private Members' Business
If we look at worker co-operatives as a whole, there are approximately, at this time in Canada, 15,000 workers who are members of such worker co-operatives, with about $300 million in annual sales. That means that we have approximately 400 worker co-operatives across the country.
These have been in Canada since the 1940s and they can be seen in such areas as heavy equipment repairs, textiles and furs, industry and wood-cutting, market gardening, building trades, and maintenance. There are actors, musicians, people in the consulting field, computer programmers, people in the print and electronic media, school bus contractors, people in towing, people in blueberry picking, cedar shingle production, restaurants, graphic art, food processing, bakeries, warehousing, and, of course, retail activities, to mention just a few.
Across the country we have a great many examples of social ownership developing. This motion suggests that it is important to protect and to extend this important role of social ownership. In the time I have left, I want to explain how it can be possible to extend this important role.
A special committee of federal and provincial officials has been meeting during over recent years. I give credit to the federal government for responding in a positive way to the suggestions of the Canadian co-operative movement for such activities. It has not moved as fast as I would have liked it to, but it has taken the issue seriously.
A special committee of federal and provincial officials has recommended three ways by which to improve, preserve, and extend this kind of social ownership. This special committee first has called on governments to provide equality of treatment so that worker co-operatives get the same kind of treatment from our financial institutions that small or medium-sized businesses receive. This would require the amending of some current legislation, some regulations that specifically limit the development of worker co-operatives.
Second, this committee has suggested that government should provide equality of opportunity. In other words, it should ensure that co-operatives are considered in the development and implementation of new programs which the government is putting into effect.
The co-operative movement, for instance, testified when the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act were being discussed, and I notice my colleague across the aisle, from Burlington, who was part of this discussion with respect to C-21. At that time the co-operative movement said: "Look, as originally drafted, these changes to the unemployment insurance regulations were not going to make it possible". At least it left it ambiguous whether it would be possible for members of worker co-operatives to use their UIC entitlement, as would be possible for those who were trying to start small enterprises to use that same entitlement to start worker co-operatives.
It has now proven to be the case that it will be possible in some of the regulatory changes which were made as a consequence of the presentations put forward by the Canadian co-operative movement. That is the kind of thing which has to take place to see that we do not have discrimination in regulations, that we have instead equality of opportunity.
Finally, this committee has suggested that governments have to overtly encourage the formation of worker co-ops. It seems to me that this requires what we as a party suggested five years ago in a report which came from an action group, which I co-chaired, called "Jobs Action Group", which aimed to provide some new bottom-up ways to increase employment opportunities, especially in some of the poorer regions of this country. To do that, however, will require some financial commitments on the part of government.
I want to finish my comments today by noting some of the suggestions which have come from the Worker-Ownership Foundation in Toronto which has set out a policy agenda direction in which government should move to provide this kind of financial support. It is something which we in this party certainly endorse very strongly.
I should say, of course, my colleague who is our spokesperson on co-operatives is here. I have to be especially careful that I do not make any mistakes in what I am saying as I carry this argument further.
The suggestion from the Worker-Ownership Foundation is that we need the implementation of a program that provides short term seed financing for specialized technical assistance people to come and work with newly establishing worker co-operatives. We also need the development of a tax credit that will partially offset the

capital gains payable by existing shareholders who sell significant blocks of shares to qualified worker-ownership groups.
We also need the development of a package of flexible debt financing instruments, loan guarantees, low interest loans, et cetera. I think if we move in this direction, the direction of encouraging this kind of social ownership, we will actually establish in this country some new innovations and some new initiatives in terms of bottom-up community development. It will give us new jobs in many parts of the country. It will preserve jobs in many parts of the country. It will give us fairer potential opportunities in many poorer regions of this country. It will, finally, and most important, give a greater sense of worker self-direction in many of the enterprises established through this form of social ownership throughout Canada.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   THE ECONOMY SOCIAL OWNERSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to address the hon. member's motion. The context of my remarks have mainly to do with the broader question of social ownership. I did not realize the hon. member would address a specific aspect, that being co-operatives. But he has, and I would like to respond specifically to some of his remarks.
I believe that his goals are laudable, that is to have people control their own destinies through taking over companies which fail, and so on. He talked about equality of treatment, equality of opportunity and, third, that the government should overtly encourage worker co-operatives or production co-operatives by means of tax credits, flexible debt financing, loan guarantees and so on.
I believe the government could perhaps give them equality of treatment and equality of opportunity through some legislative measures if there is in fact discrimination. It is my belief that there probably is not discrimination. For example, if it means doing something along the lines of the way we fund housing co-ops, then it is just another market distortion means of interfering in the economy.
I would like to take an example of one housing co-op, the Sundance housing co-op in Edmonton. It was built in 1977. It receives no less than four government subsidies. This is fine if we are to provide housing for low and
Private Members' Business
modest income people, but it distorts the housing market when we are providing housing accommodation for those high income people who are earning over $50,000. The four subsidies are a $280,000 outright grant, which is 10 per cent of the mortgage; a preferential 9.5 per cent mortgage, which was given for 50 years; a special, one time only, 1.5 per cent mortgage reduction subsidy for 50 years, which brought the mortgage rate down to 8 per cent; and the fourth subsidy, a $30,000 a year subsidy to the whole project. That is fine. Low income people and modest income people receive a subsidy. Of this $30,000 a year subsidy, people earning over whatever the cut-off rate is, I believe around $22,000, pay a modest surcharge of $72 a month.
A recent study done by CMHC said that 9 per cent of Canadians who live in these housing co-ops earn over $50,000. This is a terrible distortion of the housing market if they are taking advantage of up to four subsidies like are offered in the case of the Sundance housing co-op. If the hon. member is speaking of these types of subsidies when he talks about flexible debt financing, loan guarantees, tax credits and so on, I do not think we want anything.
Further on the matter of the Sundance housing co-op, it is my belief that the high income people should, after a period of time, when their incomes reach 50,000, move on to allow low income people or modest income people to have affordable housing. Thirty-four per cent of the people living in the Sundance housing co-op can afford a mortgage on a modest home. Why is the Government of Canada subsidizing them?
We cannot, with a $30 billion deficit each year on a debt approaching $350 billion, afford to keep subsidizing this and that and everything else. For your information, Mr. Speaker, there is a member of Parliament living in the Sundance housing co-op, the member for Edmonton East. He lives with four other people there, pays as his share less than $200 a month rent. I estimate the rent money that is paid on each unit is one-half of what it would cost in the private sector.
What happens is sometimes a clique develops which really distorts. There is a committee. They pick who comes into the co-op and once again, that is distorting the market. They are laudable goals that the co-operative movement can achieve, but sometimes by perpetuating some of these distortions and abuses of government

November 2, 1990
Private Members' Business
programs, people are discrediting the whole co-operative movement.
I would argue that social ownership is no longer the route to go. If a group of workers wants to take over a plant that is closing, they can get together and put together a business plan. They can approach a bank. The bank can lend them money. They can put a management team in place, and that is fine. The government should in no way be involved in giving them preferential treatment to distort the market in order to favour a select group of people.
I was invited two weeks ago today to address the Co-operative Council of Edmonton, Alberta. They have an annual meeting that is made up of 15 members, two of which are housing co-operatives. There are other members, which the hon. member listed. There are credit unions, farm co-operatives, workers co-operatives, consumer co-operatives and so on. T\vo hours before I was to address them, I received a phone call. I was told I could not address them because I had spoken out against housing co-operatives and they felt it was not appropriate.
In this case, a few members of housing co-operatives who are earning over $50,000 a year were offended that I suggested that they should no longer take advantage of massive government subsidies. They were really offended and said: "No, we do not want you to speak here", even though they were only two out of 15. They were discrediting the whole co-operative movement by such a petty way of approaching what would have been a very rational and reasonable discussion.
I personally support housing co-operatives and other co-operatives. Housing co-operatives are a very good way of providing housing for low and moderate income Canadians, and the Government of Canada should continue to do that. But we should in no way subsidize high income Canadians, including two members of this Chamber, to be the recipient of massive housing co-operatives.
Social ownership has distorted what we want to achieve and we no longer should be involved in this manner. If we want to provide housing support, we should have housing support that is targeted at those in need. There are growing numbers of homeless people
and low and moderate income people who need affordable housing.
The co-operative movement should look seriously at what the hon. member is talking about, getting involved and becoming more active, but he should not be asking for government subsidies or loan guarantees or for taxpayers to support them in this manner. We support them in other manners through the unemployment insurance program and so on.
In closing, I would say that social ownership is not what we as Canadians want to achieve. We want the free enterprise system to continue. It has provided a lot of growth. Individual initiative has spurred growth and economic activity.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   THE ECONOMY SOCIAL OWNERSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am thankful for the opportunity to rise and speak on this issue. As the member for Essex-Windsor is probably well aware, there are many worker co-operatives in my riding of Broadview-Greenwood. Carrot Common is one of them, and there are many others. I salute the work of these co-operatives. As the member mentioned, there is opportunity for more growth in the co-operative movement where all Canadians can be affected in a positive way.
First, I want to say that I am concerned about a couple of the tendencies that seem to creep forward from time to time where they try to put on an air of exclusivity. In other words, there are times when, if I go into the store and I do not have my co-op card with me, I do not tend to get the graciousness that one would normally get when one goes to any other store in the riding. In the area of public relations, the whole co-op movement would be much better served if those people who know it well and who practise it would be a little more approachable in the service they provide.
The member is missing a tremendous opportunity in the neighbourhood of financial services. He mentioned in his speech that the co-op movement had millions and millions of members across Canada. It would seem to me, if these members could be marshalled and organized in one or two of our principal financial institutions, that they could then use a very special kind of leverage because they were part of a co-operative financial institution. This could have dramatic effect on interest
November 2, 1990

rates, on mortgage rates, and on entrepreneurial loans to small and medium sized businesses.
One of the problems we have with the co-operative movement today is that no one has taken the time to marshal the forces of the various membership. I remember a lawyer friend of mine, Joe Pomerant, spent about three years of his life working with various aspects of the co-operative movement. He showed that if he could amalgamate the various co-operative clubs which existed in Ontario and use that buying power, he could lower vacation travel costs by as much as 30 per cent or 40 per cent. Those are substantial numbers.
That same spirit could be applied to the workforce. We are dealing in a world where we have to show world-class competitiveness. It just cannot be at the negotiating table when we are redoing our union contract. It also has to be in the quality of our work and the level of productivity in our work.
If the co-operative movement were to factor this noble objective which I support into its negotiations, its wages might be a lot lower, thereby making us much more competitive and thereby making opportunity for job creation and growth a lot easier.
In the marshalling of the co-op movement the available spin-off resources are limitless. We have never really put a tight focus on how we can use this, especially during times of recession. However, as the member from Edmonton mentioned earlier, if these co-operatives are to be organized, if they are going to be like bridge points for exclusive clubs, if they are to be used to get preferential financing and once the financing is in place, people develop, grow and move beyond the basic objective of the system, to the exclusion of others, that is not a very sound or logical way to go.
The co-operative movement, time and time again throughout history, has pulled us through some very tough times. In any riding across Canada where there is difficulty, it is only when all of us get together and pitch in that we actually pull ourselves out of some of the severe crises that we get ourselves in.
The member from Essex-Windsor, the man who is the driving force behind this motion, he should perhaps start with a large financial institution to see if by marshalling the forces of all members of the credit union movement across Canada he could consolidate that resource and, having consolidated that resource, perhaps
Private Members' Business
he could start a whole new trend in banking and interest rates. That would give credibility and trust to his objective more quickly than anything.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by thanking the hon. member for Essex- Windsor for presenting this motion, because it provides an ideal opportunity for showing how the government lived up to its promise of regional equity and justice for all Canadians, and especially how much has been done by Conservative members in Ottawa and especially by the tireless member for Roberval, the hon. Benoit Bouchard.
When this government came to power in 1984, it saw that despite the efforts of the previous Liberal government and the considerable sums of money it had spent on regional economic expansion, serious regional disparities still existed across the country. That is why our government embarked on an in-depth analysis of regional economic needs and decided to provide a framework for meeting those needs, something which had not been done before.
This new-framework approach, which was mentioned in the Speech from the Throne in the fall of 1986, was intended to correct regional imbalances and under-development, while concentrating on the most disadvantaged regions. In line with this approach, new regional development initiatives were introduced, based on the specific needs of target regions.
That is how the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and the Department of Western Economic Diversification were created while Industry, Science and Technology Canada was given the job of looking after Quebec and Ontario.
Mr. Speaker, let me explain for the information of the hon. member for Essex-Windsor how Industry, Science and Technology Canada has obviously succeeded in focusing its new economic development initiatives in the most disadvantaged areas of Quebec and Ontario by providing them too with promising opportunities.
In Quebec, on regional development, this government has developed an action program specifically aimed at achieving the goals hoped for by the hon. member for Essex-Windsor, that is job creation and lowering unem-

Private Members' Business
ployment, reduction of regional disparities between regions and technological development of businesses.
When we came into office in 1984, we agreed to pursue the industrial and regional development program, the IRDP, established in 1983 by the previous government. This program was to promote industrial and regional expansion by supporting private sector initiatives that offered the most opportunities for profitability, sustained growth and competitiveness in the international arena.
Even if the program was of national scope, the degree of assistance given to businesses varied depending on the level of social and economical development in the region where the projects were. So, the more a region was disadvantaged in terms of unemployment and income, among other things, the more assistance it might receive. So, the IRDP was taking into account the economic disparities, not only from region to region nationally, but also between different parts of the same province like Quebec.
The IRDP, by promoting the establishment of new plants and the modernization of existing ones, helped create and maintain thousand of jobs throughout Quebec. The program also had an "innovation" facet which helped promote technological innovation and development in a number of Quebec industries.
Anxious to adapt our regional development policies to the specific needs of the various regions, our government signed with the Quebec government, in 1988, a multisectorial and multiregional agreement for economic development. With a view toward harmonizing the actions of both levels of government and maximizing their impact, the agreement's main objectives were to speed the economic growth of the various regions of Quebec and increase the participation of local populations in the work force.
The five-year agreement has a budget of $820 million, $440 million of which, that is 54 per cent, coming from the federal government. I must emphasize, that the major part of the funds, $486 million, will be allocated to areas with a resource-based economy, as their industrial base is not very diversified and often fragile, and also because these areas are far from the main urban centres and have a much higher rate of unemployment. This is
particularly true of my own riding of Abitibi, and the riding of Temiscamingue, in Northern Quebec.
In areas where the economy is resource-based, initiatives come under five distinct headings: Business development, Technological development, Natural resources development, Strengthening of economic infrastructures and Human resources development.
That is why specific initiatives have been put in place in the agri-food industry, fisheries and aquaculture, as well as for the enhancement of the industrial and tourist sector. Also, we have just announced an innovations assistance program.
As for the central regions, we have established a manufacturing productivity strenghtening program, and we support seven initiatives for the development of the Montreal area. We have announced recently two programs, a depressed areas assistance program and an innovations assistance program. And the hon. member for Essex-Windsor could read in the record the statement I made in this House about the state of progress of this agreement with the province of Quebec. The hon. member will see that it is the member for Roberval, the hon. Benoit Bouchard who has done his homework and not minister Gil Remillard.
Furthermore, the federal government promotes regional development in Quebec through subsidiary development agreements within specific sectors or areas. As early as 1985, our government and that of Quebec agreed upon a set of subsidiary development agreements in forestry and mining, the agri-food industry, fisheries, tourism, home entertainment products, transportation, communications as well as science and technology.
A total of $1.4 billion has been earmarked for those various sectoral agreements. The money was divided equally between Canada and Quebec. It includes an amount of $150 million that was covered by a draft agreement and was distributed in March 1990 into seven sectoral agreements.
By the same token, we prolonged most of the sectoral agreements until March 1991. Needless to say many measures and initiatives put into place under those agreements will contribute considerably to the development of Quebec regions.

As to the Montreal region, our government recognizes it faces particular problems. The unemployment and poverty problem in the central districts of the city of Montreal is particularly worrying. We know the east and southwest districts were the most affected by plant closings and massive lay-offs in the last few years. This is why the Canadian government has been actively promoting the economic renewal of that urban district for over two years.
The Industrial Recovery Program for East End Montreal, set up in June 1988, and PRISOM, launched in September of this year, both aim at re-inforcing and diversifying local industrial structures, attracting new investments, and furthering the creation and growth of new concerns, particularly small- and medium-sized businesses. The aggregate budget for these five-year programs is $50 million.
Mr. Speaker, a word now about the positive and constructive efforts of the government in northern Ontario through FEDNOR which was established in 1987 to make sure that this region gets all the help it needs to achieve its full economic development potential. The $55 million earmarked for this five-year project represented a major commitment, as a result of which a number of businesses were set up and jobs created in the whole region.
Under FEDNOR, over $26 million in federal funds were allocated to finance some 311 projects. I must emphasize the fact that they also created and maintained nearly 2,225 jobs. The FEDNOR advisory council which is responsible for ensuring the relevance of all the FEDNOR programs to the local needs was totally involved in these contributions.
This government, in response to the very favourable reaction of the public towards FEDNOR, and in spite of budget cuts, made sure that businessmen in Northern Ontario received the assistance they needed so very much. That is the reason why an additional amount of $14 million has just been allocated to FEDNOR.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, before blaming the government for its so-called disregard for regional equity, the hon. member for Essex-Windsor should have talked to the business people in Northern Ontario
Private Members' Business
who appreciate in particular what the federal government has done so far for them through FEDNOR.
Mr. Speaker, FEDNOR has greatly helped business people in Northern areas meet the challenge and achieve their full potential. Under a special provision dealing with acquisition, FEDNOR is helping a whole series of Northern Ontario businesses sell their wares to the federal government.
Hardly a few weeks ago, representatives from over 80 businesses in 25 Northern Ontario communities came on a trade mission to the National Capital to present a sort of vista of Northern Ontario. This mission, sponsored and organized by FEDNOR, in co-operation with Supply and Services Canada, was intended to help Northern suppliers do business with the federal government.
Mr. Speaker, government activities in Northeastern Ontario, which is going through a difficult period, are worthy of note. In the Temiscamingue area, for instance, FEDNOR representatives have helped speed up processing of applications for regional assistance. Thanks to FEDNOR, investments by Pyrok and Dymond Clay will make a major contribution to the region's economy. We could name several programs, including agriculture, but above all, Mr. Speaker, this government has played a major role in recognizing the importance of the economy of Northern Ontario and Northern Quebec. My point is, Madam Speaker, that our approach has been successful. In fact, we are nearing our goal, which is equality for all Canadians. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   THE ECONOMY SOCIAL OWNERSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion put forward by the hon. member for Essex- Windsor is interesting and intriguing and I must just read it again so that we will see where we are going.
The motion reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of protecting and extending the important role of social ownership in the economy, in order to achieve the social goals of full employment, regional equity, technological development and equality among Canadians.
I appreciate the hon. member's desire for full employment in Canada, and I understand and respect the hon. member's wish to invest in Canadian men and women

Private Members' Business
and provide them with training and retraining opportunities that will allow them to participate fully in a thriving economy.
I know that he is sincere in putting forward his motion and his ambition to build a strong and competitive future for our country through full employment.
I would like to point out to him that laudable though his intentions may be, the motion he has placed before the House displays a lack of understanding about what is feasible in a land as diverse and complex as Canada. It shows a disturbing inability to grasp the complexities of our labour market.
I would like also to remind the hon. member that this government has always understood the importance of investing in our citizens. Indeed, we are at this moment making the very types of social investment he advocates in his motion. These investments come in the form of training and retraining Canadian workers in programs offered through the Canadian Jobs Strategy and our Labour Force Development Strategy.
We have always maintained that the failure to preserve a competitive workforce would have dire consequences not only for the individuals who lost their jobs but for Canada's economic prospects as well. That is why we have dedicated more dollars to job training and skill enhancement than any government in the history of Canada.
I noticed that the hon. member's motion did not define "full employment". This is understandable. Our organizations such as the Canada Employment and Immigration Advisory Council which is also keen to see full employment has stated: "It would be impossible to come up with a definition of full employment with which everyone would agree."
In effect, the Advisory Council acknowledged that defining full employment would be as complicated as Rubic's cube. In its recent report on unemployment, the Canada Employment and Immigration Advisory Council suggested that the figure of 4 per cent unemployment might be considered full employment.
It is our view that the selection of a single unemployment target such as 4 per cent is not feasible nor is it realistic, because Canada remains a country of great regional diversity. Governments cannot push a button to replenish the cod stocks in the Atlantic nor force
automobile plants to the Gaspe coast where unemployment in particularly severe.
On top of that, Canada like the rest of the industrialized world, is facing rapid economic changes as international trading and manufacturing patterns evolve to adjust to a much more dynamic and unpredictable global market.
The choice of targets such as 4 per cent for full employment can also be very misleading. In fact, the unemployment rate of 4 per cent or less can even mask great disparities.
When the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood was making his remarks in this debate, he made reference to financial institutions that may be able to present programs and have loans, mortgages and other financial transactions at a lesser rate than some of our banks and trust companies today.
I might say that my son is employed with Van City Savings and Loans in Vancouver, which I believe is the largest credit union in the world. It competes very well in that vibrant financial market in Vancouver with some pretty large numbers. It has done very well, but I might also note that most of the chief executive officers have come from some pretty large corporations to direct it and to give it good advice as it carries on down the road.
There are good areas for it. But it is not the workers' nirvana. Co-operatives have many forms.
At one time in business I formed a company where I had all the shareholders, who were mainly the employees, with the same amount of common stock. My investment differential was in the preferred shares. They said as long as the company made a profit and paid a dividend out of current earnings, that is the way it would run. But if the company lost money for two consecutive years, then the preferred shares would have voting power and the direction of the company could be changed. There are many forms that a co-operative can take. It is not the answer to all things in business, but it does have a place to play.
Let us compare the year 1967 in Canada, when the unemployment rate was 3.8 per cent to 1988, when the unemployment rate was 7.8 per cent. A single comparison of the two numbers would suggest that Canadians were better off in 1967 than they were in 1988.
November 2, 1990

After all, if we stick to the Advisory Council's definition of full employment in 1967, we were actually within the unemployment rate of 3.8 per cent. However, a closer look at the numbers suggests that everything is not quite so rosy, particularly when we compare the two years to the numbers of people who held full time, year-round jobs.
In 1967, the year with apparent full employment, 39 per cent of the population 15 years of age and older worked full time all year. But in 1988, a full 5 per cent more, or 44 per cent of the population held full time jobs year-round.
Let us compare what this has meant in dollars and cents for Canadians. And let's adjust the comparison to 1988 dollars so there will be no confusion.
In 1967, the year that meets the Advisory Council's definition of full employment, 14 per cent of the Canadian population enjoyed adjusted annual earnings of $25,000 or more. But in 1988, when we had an unemployment rate of 7.8 per cent, more than 25 per cent of the youth and adult population earned that much. Now, were we closer to full employment in 1967 or in 1988? Which would you choose?
What I am pointing out to the hon. member, Mr. Speaker, is that full employment is much more complicated than his motion suggests.
This government believes that increased employment is possible and that the federal government has a significant role in achieving this goal. The government has recently authorized a new ceiling of $346 million for training measures in 1990. That is more money than we have ever before set aside for training in the past.
Private Members' Business
Because of these allocations, people who would otherwise have been looking for work now have the opportunity to increase their skills to find the work they want. This emphasis on active intervention such as training and re-employment, rather than passive income support, is endorsed by all member countries of the OECD. Our goal is to apportion even a greater amount of our labour market programming towards this end.
This change in emphasis, Mr. Speaker, lies at the heart of the Labour Force Development Strategy. The Labour Force Development Strategy will dedicate more dollars to job training and skill enhancement than ever before. A total of $800 million is being reallocated to expand the developmental use of unemployment insurance. The increased expenditures on active programs will raise our active mix of labour market programming from 25 per cent to 40 per cent.
The expanded developmental use of unemployment insurance funds will allow for more training, mobility, self-employment and other re-employment strategies, practical measures that will provide long-term benefit to unemployed Canadians.
